issues.body: Purpose of Issue is to track total norm grad growth on Hero Run, in case an intervention is needed: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng Our prior 129B-A16B MoE on 1T tokens showed clean loss descent over the run, with a grad that peaked at about 38% into run. The equivalent point in this run would be about step 150k. We see step change in slope of the final rms norm when moving to dropless: However the prior 1e23 run had large final rms norm growth and trained fine: The total grad is driven 95% by the output projection. Output proj sits in AdamH. Incoming activation goes through rms norm and gated norm. Likely take no intervention as long as loss curve looks good, given data from prior 129B-A16B. If we were to see loss curve degrade, potential interventions would be: - higher logit z loss. - weight decay on final rms-norm. - lower LR on lm_head. It is not obvious that any of these would be a 'fix', or even that there is a problem to fix. As a result, would want to compare to baseline for at least 1 day of steps. The growth is specifically in just the lm_head:

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Frozen-gradient probes at checkpoint 101,316 rule out a kernel artifact and a direct effect of dropping; the lm_head rise is a trajectory effect, and the lm_head gradient is tangential. No intervention recommended on this evidence. Details below; the same material was filed as #9149 before this issue was seen, and that issue is now closed in favour of this one.

Method: restore the hero checkpoint at step 101,316 on one NVL72 rack, take no updates, and compute the training gradient on the hero's own next six batches under three variants: the production ragged transport on QuACK 0.6.4, the same transport on the XLA `ragged_dot` fallback (exact sigmoid), and the pooled-wave transport at capacity factor 1.15 (3.4% drops). Each also with the logit z-loss off. For every parameter the probe records the gradient norm, the weight norm and their inner product. Records are under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/mwittmann/grad-norm-20260914/`; W&B runs `gradnorm-101316-ragged-v2-20260914` and `gradnorm-101316-pooled-20260914` in `marin_moe`. First-batch values; the pattern holds on all six.

| variant | loss | grad total | lm_head grad | cos(grad, W) lm_head | final_norm gain grad |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ragged, QuACK 0.6.4 (production) | 1.25651 | 0.6024 | 0.5735 | −4.9e-5 | 4.4e-4 |
| ragged, QuACK, z-loss off | 1.25614 | 0.6015 | 0.5720 | −4.9e-5 | 4.7e-4 |
| ragged, XLA `ragged_dot` fallback | 1.25652 | 0.6019 | 0.5736 | −4.9e-5 | 4.4e-4 |
| pooled-wave cf 1.15 (drops on) | 1.26849 | 0.6047 | 0.5665 | −1.0e-4 | 4.8e-4 |

The lm_head gradient is tangential. Its cosine with the weights is −5e-5 on every batch and variant, so the radial (logit temperature) component is a few parts in 10⁵ of the norm, and the final-norm gain sits near its optimum (cosine −0.07 on a 4.5e-4 gradient). Turning the z-loss off changes the lm_head gradient by 0.28%. So the growth is a steepening of the loss along model-changing lm_head directions; it is not a temperature pull that the z-loss or a final-norm weight decay would be absorbing.

Kernels: QuACK and the XLA fallback agree on the loss to 1e-5, on the lm_head gradient to 1e-4, and on expert weights, latent projections and attention matrices to about 1%. The lm_head gradient does not pass through the expert backward, so an expert-kernel error cannot move it directly. The hero's per-tensor gradient history is also continuous across the switch from the pooled einsum path to QuACK at 81,716. One caveat: the RMSNorm gain gradients (latent_norm about 1e-2, token embeddings about 1e-3) differ between the two kernels by up to 7× on some batches in either direction (ratios 6.9, 0.93, 1.1, 0.99, 0.41, 0.26). They are cancellation-dominated sums that flip under QuACK's 0.5% approximate SwiGLU, contribute under 1e-3 of the squared total, and the same executable reproduces them to 6e-3. A systematic component is not excluded and is cheap to test by saving the gain-gradient vectors from both kernels and an fp32 reference on the same batches.

Dropping has no direct effect at fixed parameters: the pooled-wave arm gives a lm_head gradient 1.2% below the ragged one and a total 0.4% above it, averaged over the six batches. Over the paired 200-step replay at 81,716 the ragged-to-pooled lm_head ratio was 1.06 ± 0.07 across 20 samples. The pooled arm's loss is 0.012 nats worse; the offset was 0.0065 at the switch, so the model has grown more dependent on complete expert outputs.

From W&B: the lm_head share of the squared total went from 84% at 58k to 95% at 100k; every other parameter group is flat, including the routed expert weights (0.0094 to 0.0104). The slope of the total per 1k steps was 0.0040 (62–72k), 0.0062 (72–82k), 0.0133 (82–91k) and 0.0085 (91–101k), so it was already accelerating before the switch and has been falling since. The d768 rungs trained dropless from scratch (`l2-abl-d768-ragged` vs `l2-abl-d768-ep`; `mhep-main-c13d1-d768-20260902` vs `rav-ladder-d768-v2`) show equal or lower gradient norms than pooled-wave in every tenth of the run and the same final-norm gain trajectory within 1%, so dropless training does not raise the norm in general; the effect is tied to switching a model that had adapted to noisy experts.

Reading: among the bundled changes at 81,716 (transport, kernels, fp32 weights on device, PJRT wheel), the transport is the only one that alters what the model computes beyond rounding, so the slope change is attributable by elimination to the reduced dropping acting through the trajectory. A demonstration would need paired multi-thousand-step continuations from 81,716, which does not look worth the compute. Today's data-mixture swap will move the norm on its own, so the slope is best judged from a new post-swap window. The QuACK 0.6.1 to 0.6.4 frozen-state probe in the #8959 validation found the two versions' gradient norms identical to 3e-6 relative, for reference on the earlier +10% A/B difference.

issues.title: Hero Run: Total Grad Norm Growth

issues.author: mcwitt-agent
issues.body:
## TL;DR

The hero's gradient norm has grown from 0.28 (step 58k) to 0.59 (step 100k), with the slope roughly doubling after the switch to the near-dropless ragged EP transport at step 81,716. By step 100k the lm_head carries 95% of the squared norm; every other parameter group is flat. Three one-rack frozen-gradient probes at checkpoint 101,316 give the same lm_head gradient from the same state on the production QuACK kernels, the XLA `ragged_dot` fallback, and the pooled-wave transport with 3.4% drops (0.5735 / 0.5736 / 0.5665), and the gradient's radial component is zero (cosine with the weights −5e-5). The rise is a trajectory effect of training without drops, attributable by elimination among the bundled changes. No intervention is recommended; loss and dropless Paloma are on track and the post-switch slope is falling.

## Description

`grad/norm/total` on [hero-ragged_a2a-nccl2307-ep-step81k](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-ragged_a2a-nccl2307-ep-step81k) rose faster after the ragged EP redeploy (#8506, #9043). Larry Dial raised it on Discord on 2026-09-13 ([thread](https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1548520475397718068/1548520790742274108)) with the reading that the lm_head dominates through the final RMS-norm gain and that near-dropless routing lets the model make sharper predictions. The competing concern was a numerical or correctness issue in the QuACK expert MLP kernels, which the pooled-wave hero never ran (its expert MLP is an XLA einsum), so the switch at 81,716 was also the hero's first step on QuACK.

2000-step windowed medians from W&B:

| window | transport | grad total | lm_head | lm_head share of ‖g‖² | final_norm gain ‖w‖ | drop fraction |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 58k | pooled | 0.282 | 0.259 | 0.84 | 322 | 3.4e-2 |
| 80k | pooled | 0.372 | 0.352 | 0.90 | 342 | 3.4e-2 |
| 82k | ragged | 0.407 | 0.387 | 0.91 | 344 | 7.9e-5 |
| 100k | ragged | 0.586 | 0.573 | 0.95 | 368 | 1.1e-4 |

Slope of the total per 1k steps: 0.0040 (62–72k), 0.0062 (72–82k), 0.0133 (82–91k), 0.0085 (91–101k). Over the paired 200-step replay at 81,716 the norms were 0.373 (pooled) and 0.380 (ragged). Expert-weight gradient aggregates moved from 0.0094 to 0.0104 over 58k–100k.

The d768 rungs trained dropless from scratch show no such effect: `l2-abl-d768-ragged` has an equal or lower gradient norm than `l2-abl-d768-ep` in every tenth of the run and the same final-norm gain trajectory within 1%; the `rav-ladder-d768-v2` / `mhep-main-c13d1-d768-20260902` pair shows the same ordering.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Determine whether the lm_head gradient rise is attributable to reduced token dropping alone, and exclude a kernel error in the ragged EP expert MLP.

## Status

Frozen-gradient probes at checkpoint 101,316 (copied to `s3://hero-checkpoints/tmp/ttl=7d/grad-norm-20260914/step-101316`), one NVL72 rack, no parameter updates, the hero's own next six batches. Records: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/mwittmann/grad-norm-20260914/`. First-batch values; the pattern holds on all six.

| variant | loss | grad total | lm_head grad | cos(grad, W) lm_head | final_norm gain grad |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ragged, QuACK 0.6.4 (production) | 1.25651 | 0.6024 | 0.5735 | −4.9e-5 | 4.4e-4 |
| ragged, QuACK, z-loss off | 1.25614 | 0.6015 | 0.5720 | −4.9e-5 | 4.7e-4 |
| ragged, XLA `ragged_dot` fallback | 1.25652 | 0.6019 | 0.5736 | −4.9e-5 | 4.4e-4 |
| pooled-wave cf 1.15 (drops on) | 1.26849 | 0.6047 | 0.5665 | −1.0e-4 | 4.8e-4 |

Findings:

- The lm_head gradient is tangential. Its cosine with the weights is −5e-5 on every batch and variant, so the radial (logit temperature) component is a few parts in 10⁵ of the norm, and the final-norm gain sits near its optimum (cosine −0.07 on a 4.5e-4 gradient). The z-loss accounts for 0.28% of the lm_head gradient.
- QuACK and the XLA fallback agree on the loss to 1e-5, the lm_head gradient to 1e-4, and expert weights, latent projections and attention matrices to about 1%. The lm_head gradient does not pass through the expert backward, so an expert-kernel error cannot move it directly. The hero's per-tensor gradient history is continuous across the einsum-to-QuACK switch (latent_norm gain gradient paired ratio 0.88).
- The RMSNorm gain gradients (latent_norm about 1e-2, token embeddings about 1e-3) differ between the two kernels by up to 7× on some batches, in either direction (ratios 6.9, 0.93, 1.1, 0.99, 0.41, 0.26 across the six). They are cancellation-dominated sums over 4M tokens that flip under QuACK's 0.5% approximate SwiGLU; the same executable reproduces them to 6e-3. Those gains train on a signal that bf16 details decide, in either path. Relevant to #9077, whose kernel migration will change their trajectories.
- Dropping has no direct effect at fixed parameters: the pooled-wave arm gives a lm_head gradient 1.2% below the ragged one and a total 0.4% above it, averaged over six batches. Its loss is 0.012 nats worse; the offset was 0.0065 at the switch, so the model has grown more dependent on complete expert outputs.
- The QuACK 0.6.1 to 0.6.4 frozen-state probe in the #8959 validation found the two versions' gradient norms identical to 3e-6 relative, and the 100-step hero A/B difference there (+10% mean) was trajectory variance.

Reading: the rise is a trajectory effect and predates the switch. Among the bundled changes at 81,716 (transport, kernels, fp32 weights on device, PJRT wheel), the transport is the only one that alters what the model computes beyond rounding, so the slope change is attributable to the reduced dropping. The from-scratch d768 pairs show it is tied to switching a model that had adapted to noisy experts, and no rung reproduces the hero's continued rise at 26% of the run (rungs peak at 10–25% and decay with the LR schedule). MuonH, AdamH and Adam normalize the gradient and the hero applies no clipping, so the magnitude does not change the step. The quantities to watch are train loss and the dropless Paloma aggregate; Larry's trigger for action is a norm past 5 with a diverging loss, at which point the plan is an earlier checkpoint with a stronger z-loss or weight decay on the final norm. Today's data-mixture swap will move the norm on its own, so the slope should be judged from a new post-swap window.

Not done, and not recommended on current evidence: paired multi-thousand-step continuations from 81,716 to split the bundle strictly (about 11 rack-hours per arm). A cheaper optional test, if the norm keeps climbing past the historical 1.5 on the lm_head, is a mid-run switch at d768: restore the pooled rung at 25% and continue on ragged and pooled.

## Links

* W&B: [hero-ragged_a2a-nccl2307-ep-step81k](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-ragged_a2a-nccl2307-ep-step81k), [hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k), probe runs `gradnorm-101316-ragged-v2-20260914` and `gradnorm-101316-pooled-20260914` in `marin_moe` (group `grad-norm-probe`)
* Discord: [tracking grad norm thread](https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1548520475397718068/1548520790742274108)
* Related: #8435, #8506, #8818, #8959, #9077
* Brief with charts (private artifact, shareable on request): https://claude.ai/code/artifact/a78852dc-9b11-479a-a357-f81431fa7576

## Decision Log

* 2026-09-14: no intervention on the hero; watch loss and dropless Paloma; re-baseline the slope after the mixture swap.

## Conclusion

The lm_head gradient rise is a trajectory effect of training without token drops on a model that had adapted to them. It is not a kernel artifact, not a direct effect of dropping, and not a logit-temperature pull. Stated with the caveat that the bundled changes were separated by elimination and fixed-state probes, not by paired continuations.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
Deduplicate TaskTrove tasks within each published source before a later export. The default split contains 1,739,326 task archives across 93 non-deprecated sources. The task instruction is `instruction.md` inside the gzip-compressed tar stored in `task_binary`.

Done when:
- A Zephyr pipeline reads each source's `tasks.parquet` by row group and hashes the exact UTF-8 bytes of `instruction.md`.
- Duplicate decisions are grouped by source and instruction hash; the shortest path is retained as the canonical task.
- Sparse duplicate markers, canonical paths, hashes, and a summary are written under the active region-local Marin storage prefix.
- The result contains enough provenance to export a filtered TaskTrove dataset without recomputing instruction hashes.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read AGENTS.md, fix-issue, commit skills
- [x] Confirm actionability and scope
- [x] Map TaskTrove data model (`tasks.parquet`, `task_binary`, `instruction.md`)
- [x] Study Zephyr Dataset API and pipeline conventions
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight (no existing PR/pipeline)
- [x] Post approach for human review (new feature > 100 lines → no PR)

**Research**

TaskTrove is the HF dataset `open-thoughts/TaskTrove`. Each non-deprecated source is a directory holding a `tasks.parquet`; the [manifest builder](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/marina/apps/tasktrove/manifest.py#L30-L59) already enumerates them (skipping `*/deprecated`) and reads the parquet footer per source. Each row carries a `path` (string) and a `task_binary` cell that is a base64/gzip tar; the [web loader](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/marina/apps/tasktrove/web/src/trove.ts#L86-L97) shows the decode chain (base64 → gunzip → tar entries), with `instruction.md` living inside the archive. No dedup pipeline exists today; the decontam corpus builder reads `instruction.md` only from a different (terminal-bench zip) source, so there is nothing to reuse directly. Preflight found no open PR or overlapping issue.

**Scope**

This is a net-new Zephyr pipeline (source enumeration, per-task tar extraction + hashing, a shuffle/group, and provenance outputs), comfortably over 100 lines. Per the task rules I am not opening a PR; this is a proposed design for a human to confirm before implementation.

**Proposed approach**

1. **Enumerate sources** — factor the non-deprecated listing out of `manifest.py` (or mirror it) to get the 93 source dirs and their `tasks.parquet` paths.
2. **Hash instructions by row group** — `Dataset.load_parquet(columns=["path", "task_binary"], approx_shard_bytes=...)` streams at row-group granularity ([dataset.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/zephyr/src/zephyr/dataset.py#L643-L672)). A `map` gunzips each `task_binary`, reads `instruction.md` from the tar, and emits `{source, path, hash=sha256(exact utf-8 bytes)}`. Hash the raw bytes before any decode to honor "exact UTF-8 bytes".
3. **Choose canonical per (source, hash)** — `group_by(key=(source, hash), reducer=...)` where the reducer keeps the shortest `path` (lexicographic tie-break) as canonical and emits a sparse marker for every other member. Group by `(source, hash)` so dedup never crosses source boundaries.
4. **Write provenance** — write parquet under the region-local prefix from [`marin_prefix()`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem/cluster_config.py#L396): sparse duplicate markers (`source, path, hash, canonical_path`), the canonical map, and a per-source summary (row count, unique count, duplicates removed). Carry enough columns that a downstream export filters to canonicals without re-reading `task_binary` or recomputing hashes.

Run via `ZephyrContext(...).execute(...)` following [`experiments/datakit/reference_pipeline.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/datakit/reference_pipeline.py#L1112-L1127); the global-dedup shuffle shape in `experiments/datakit/global_exact_dedup.py` is the closest existing precedent.

**Questions for a maintainer**

- **Location:** new module under `experiments/datakit/` (e.g. `tasktrove_dedup.py`), or elsewhere?
- **Output format/layout:** parquet as above, and a preferred sub-prefix under `marin_prefix()`?
- **Missing/duplicate `instruction.md`:** fail hard, or record a sentinel and skip? (Prefer failing hard per repo error-handling norms unless real data has gaps.)
- Should the canonical also account for the `deprecated/` variants, or strictly the 93 non-deprecated sources as stated?

issues.author: atqamar
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Continue the async non-agentic RL work from #8936 as a structured research program: one
evaluation/task system with a frozen answer contract, a Qwen3-0.6B screening ladder, a MoE rung
(Qwen3-30B-A3B) used only where a dense model cannot answer, and Snowball confirmation with a
pre-registered non-inferiority margin. Weight-sync cost, the largest measured lever at Snowball
scale, is treated as engineering with bit-identical proofs, not as a research question.

## Description

The first epic (#8936) built the async trainer path, the telemetry, and the Grafana dashboard,
and produced controlled 25- and 100-update comparisons on Qwen3-0.6B and Snowball. It also found
that raw GSM8K reward hides nontermination (Snowball scored 120/128 raw with 64 completed
answers), that the cadence lever changes staleness and cost together, and that the drift
metric conflates engine mismatch with staleness. This epic starts from that evidence with a
narrative structure: goal → sub-goals → hypotheses → experiments, each experiment with a fixed
design bucket, a done-when, and a kill criterion.

Scope: non-agentic math; Megatron trainer; vLLM inference with existing flags only; H100.
Out of scope: agentic tasks, vLLM implementation work, GB200.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Snowball RL can run faster in wall-clock and GPU-hours at non-inferior held-out quality by
decoupling the trainer from rollout workers, and there is a measurable safe range of off-policy
age. A speedup is a hypothesis to test; the completion criterion is evidence with confidence
intervals and an operating recommendation.

Sub-goals: trustworthy measurement · a cost model of where training time goes · cheap weight
sync · off-policy tolerance · system balance (cadence, GPU split, admission) ·
learning-quality validity · trainer memory and speed · a scale ladder from Qwen3-0.6B to Snowball.

## How to read this thread

One comment per milestone or per experiment. Each comment has four parts: what we did and why,
results (with numbers and intervals), what this means, and what comes next. Provenance (commits,
receipts, W&B links, audit gates) is in a collapsed block at the end of each comment.

## Status

(one line per milestone, newest first)

- Milestone 1 — prior runs closed out: the isolated-TIS analysis and the canonical results table
  are posted; no configuration graduates on a single seed.
- Milestone 0 — program started: execution branches `atqamar/async-non-agentic-rl-v2` created
  from MarinSkyRL `fa6aae36` / Marin `eb85a25675`; preflight passed; answer contract frozen.

## Milestones

0 program started · 1 prior runs closed out · 2 evaluation and task system in place · 3
telemetry and pause fix landed · 4 answer contract and tasks fixed · 5 weight sync under 1.5 s
with bit-identical proof · 6 correction chosen and safe-bound rule · 7 learner-size decision · 8
system balance measured · 9 MoE-rung verdict · 10 final tradeoff statement with confidence intervals.

## Glossary

- **Cadence C** — sync weights to the rollout workers every C optimizer updates.
- **Age A** — the maximum number of updates a rollout group may lag the trainer and still be used.
- **P/I** — learner GPUs / inference GPUs.
- **Objectives** — behaviour-clip (BC), plain PPO (REG), PPO with truncated importance sampling
  (REG+TIS), and the masked/second-moment corrections to be added.
- **Three cost axes** — optimizer updates, consumed tokens, and GPU-hours plus core seconds.
- **Three quality scores** — the verifier's raw reward; the completed score (correct *and* the
  response ended on its own, not at the token cap), which is the ranking metric; and a semantic
  score (final answer checked after the thinking boundary).
- **Staleness** — policy-version lag in optimizer updates unless stated otherwise.

## Links

- Prior epic: #8936 (results that carry over are in the milestone-1 comments).
- Reference log this format follows: #8765.

## Decision Log

- 2026-09-08 — Eval battery replaces the locked 1,191-row GSM8K window with GSM8K-Platinum + MATH
  items (window at ceiling, some mislabeled items, informative signal collapses after 60
  updates); the old window stays as the legacy battery for closing the prior confirmation.
- 2026-09-08 — Weight-sync design: shard-to-shard NCCL send/recv (expert weights are already in
  vLLM's layout on the trainer under TP1/EP8); delta weight sync gated on density and on
  sync still mattering afterwards.
- 2026-09-08 — Non-inferiority margin: 2 pp on the completed score (default, revisable before the
  Snowball quality stage); seed count derived from the measured Snowball seed spread before
  confirmation launches.

cadences × three objectives) but never analysed it. The question it can answer is whether the
truncated-importance-sampling correction (TIS) helps quality when rollouts are up to three
updates stale, which matters because letting rollouts go stale is how async training gets its
speed. We audited all six runs and compared the arms in pairs on the completed score (correct
*and* the response ended on its own), the ranking metric for this program. This is a historical
run: one training seed, the legacy GSM8K contract, and the small 128-question development set.

Paired contrasts on the completed score (98.75% paired percentile-bootstrap intervals, which
give simultaneous 95% coverage for the four comparisons; 100,000 draws; exact two-sided
McNemar p-values, Holm-adjusted):

| contrast | delta pp | simultaneous 95% interval | Holm-adjusted p |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| cadence 1: PPO+TIS − plain PPO | +75.00 | [+64.84, +84.38] | 1.0e-28 |
| cadence 1: behaviour-clip − plain PPO | +68.75 | [+58.59, +78.91] | 1.9e-26 |

[Quality versus updates, consumed tokens and core time; audited JSON and analysis source](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/artifacts/analysis/async-rl-v2-e0-audited-results/v0).

**What this means.**
1. At cadence 4 (the configuration that saves time), the TIS correction is worth +7.8 pp on
   completed answers with an interval that includes zero, and behaviour-clip is worth +6.3 pp,
   also including zero. On one seed this is not a resolved benefit.
2. At cadence 1, plain PPO's failure is almost entirely nontermination: it scored 94/128 on raw
   reward but only 2/128 completed, with 126/128 responses cut off at the token cap. Both
   corrections fix that (+75 and +69 pp, well outside the intervals). So the correction's
   clearest effect is on whether answers finish, not on whether they are right.
3. Fixed update counts are not equal work: consumed tokens range 5.4M–12.4M across arms, so the
   shorter core times at cadence 4 are not an equal-token speedup, and the group ages were not
   randomised. No configuration graduates from this analysis.

**Next.** Measure how much evaluation is needed to separate arms (the power calibration), then
run the staleness ladders on Qwen with two seeds and the new evaluation battery, where these
contrasts get real intervals. Milestone 1 (prior runs closed out) follows once the canonical
results table is posted.

comments.body:
🤖 Task pool built: nine parquet views with train/dev/held-out locks, verified by readback

**What we did and why.** Every experiment in this program samples its prompts from one
versioned pool rather than from whatever rows a recipe happened to slice, so that arms and
seeds compare on identical questions and held-out sets stay held out. This step built that pool:
each prompt carries a content hash, an answer type, the contract it is scored under, a licence
field, its split, and its token count under both models' templates, and the held-out rows are
locked in a manifest the sampler cannot cross.

**Results.** The pool artifact was written and read back: `KE1_ARTIFACT_READBACK_PASS`, all nine
parquet views and the split locks verified against the candidate manifest
`d39aa170289c9637427bb2f6a829b49321875aa1ebc054fbcda7150bd2482cc1`. Independent pool and sampler
tests: `21 passed in 20.19s`.

**What this means.** Prompt identity is now a hash, not a row index, so pairing across arms and
seeds is exact and reordering a file cannot silently break a comparison.

**Next.** The final evaluation battery and the remaining eval-system gates (scorer, harness,
difficulty ratings), towards milestone 2, "evaluation and task system in place".

comments.author: atqamar
comments.body:
🤖 Seeded sampler admits only audited prompts; removing that check fails three tests

**What we did and why.** Experiments request prompts through one function, `sample(pool, bins,
n, seed, model, split)`, which must be deterministic and must refuse two things: crossing a
split boundary, and returning a prompt whose statement or gold answer has not passed the pool
audit. Without the second refusal, a mislabeled question could enter a training or evaluation
set and quietly bias a comparison.

**Results.** `KE3_ACCEPT_ONLY_MUTATION_PASS`: with the audit-eligibility check removed, three
tests fail; with it restored the suite passes 21 tests, and an independent replay also passes 21.
Sampling now requires an accepted audit status bound to the immutable manifest and the verifier;
prompts whose audit entry is missing, pending, flagged, rejected, or belongs to another manifest
cannot enter a sample.

**What this means.** The sampler is proven to bite: the test that guards audit eligibility was
shown to fail when the guard is removed, which is the standard this program holds every gate to.

**Next.** The scorer and harness gates, then the difficulty-rating pass for both models, towards
milestone 2.

🤖 Syncing every 4 updates reduces Snowball core time by 29.3%, but three seeds do not establish equal answer quality

**What we did and why.** We completed the missing run in the legacy Snowball comparison and audited all three seed pairs. The question is whether syncing weights less often makes training faster while preserving completed answers, a prerequisite for recommending an asynchronous operating range. Both configurations trained for 100 updates with behaviour clipping: sync every 2 updates with maximum age 1, versus every 4 updates with maximum age 3. Evaluation used the same locked 1,191 GSM8K questions at the start and finish.

**Results.**

Completed score means the legacy binary verifier marked the answer correct and its stop label was accepted. Truncation means the generation hit its length cap. Semantic scoring is unavailable for these historical dumps.

| cadence and seed | updates | consumed tokens | core s | task H100h | completed score | semantic | trunc % | group age mean/p95 | min ESS fraction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---|---:|
| 2, seed 17 | 100 | 14,081,797 | 3759.33 | 59.3357 | 200/1191 | NA | 82.70 | 0.50/1 | 0.98897 |
| 2, seed 29 | 100 | 12,293,213 | 3594.76 | 57.6094 | 374/1191 | NA | 67.93 | 0.50/1 | 0.96900 |
| 2, seed 43 | 100 | 14,120,429 | 3768.46 | 58.5634 | 1024/1191 | NA | 7.89 | 0.50/1 | 0.48478 |
| 4, seed 17 | 100 | 18,793,379 | 2874.52 | 49.3480 | 510/1191 | NA | 56.00 | 1.50/3 | 0.98516 |
| 4, seed 29 | 100 | 15,837,574 | 2663.95 | 47.2133 | 6/1191 | NA | 99.41 | 1.50/3 | 0.94917 |
| 4, seed 43 | 100 | 12,043,386 | 2323.28 | 42.4302 | 1056/1191 | NA | 6.88 | 1.50/3 | 0.97464 |

The completed-score differences for cadence 4 minus cadence 2 are **+26.03, −30.90, and +2.69 percentage points**, averaging **−0.73 pp**.

| uncertainty calculation | 95% interval for the mean completed-score difference |
|---|---|
| Paired questions, conditional on these three fixed training seeds | [−2.27, +0.81] pp |
| Paired training-seed effects, fixed question battery, Student-t with 2 degrees of freedom | [−71.82, +70.36] pp |

The question interval uses 10,000 paired bootstrap draws and does not measure uncertainty over new training seeds. The seed interval assumes approximately normal seed effects, which cannot be checked with three seeds; its width exposes how little these runs establish about reproducibility. Both lower bounds fall below the approved −2 pp non-inferiority margin.

Across the three seeds, cadence 4 uses **7,861.75 versus 11,122.55 core seconds** (29.3% less), **138.99 versus 175.51 task H100-hours** (20.8% less), and **46.67 versus 40.50 million consumed response tokens** (15.3% more). These are fixed-update comparisons, not equal-token speedups. The six-run cost is **314.50 H100-hours**, of which **42.43** is the newly executed candidate; the other five runs are inherited.

[Quality versus updates, consumed tokens and core time; audited summary and source](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/artifacts/analysis/async-rl-v2-e02-audited-results/v0).

**What this means.** The slower weight-sync schedule saves measured training time, but answer completion changes direction across seeds, so equal quality is **undecided** and no configuration graduates. Raw verifier reward hides the failure: the cadence-4 seed-29 run has 1,080 raw-correct answers but only 6 completed-correct answers, with 1,184 responses truncated. Sync cadence and permitted age changed together, actual consumed training order was not verified, and these historical runs cannot identify a causal age threshold.

**Next.** Finish the evaluation and task system, calibrate its power, and address nontermination before ranking new schedules. The next milestone is **evaluation and task system in place**; subsequent confirmation will use a frozen protocol and enough training seeds to support the quality decision.

comments.author: atqamar
comments.body:
🤖 Weight sync takes a median 20.226 seconds; receiver GPU telemetry is incomplete

**What we did and why.** We measured where Snowball spends time syncing updated weights to its rollout workers, to guide faster training at the same answer quality (E3.0). The run kept the existing five-second pause grace and tensor-by-tensor transfer behavior, using 32 learner and eight inference H100s for five updates. A 128-row training slice with zero data-loader workers exercised an epoch reset, while greedy evaluation ran on the same 128 development rows before training and after update five.

**Results.** [Audited JSON, three vector plots, and reproducible inputs](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/artifacts/analysis/async-rl-v2-weight-sync-baseline/v0) accompany the tables below.

All five updates, both evaluation dumps, and all five GPU tasks completed successfully. The run consumed 698,807 response tokens in 281.748 core seconds and cost 9.522493333 task H100-hours, including startup and evaluation.

| Whole-operation wall time | Median seconds | p95 seconds |
|---|---:|---:|
| Pause generation | 5.151 | 5.502 |
| Weight broadcast | 14.955 | 15.176 |
| Complete weight sync | 20.226 | 20.513 |
| Derived trainer stall | 20.154 | 20.434 |

Each row contains the five post-update syncs; startup is retained in the audit but excluded from these summaries. The stall proxy is the existing whole-sync wall time minus the host-side NCCL-send span; it is not GPU idle time. These are descriptive within-run quantiles, without a paired effect estimate or a confidence interval for a speedup.

| Stage | Wall median / p95, seconds | CUDA-event median / p95, milliseconds | Observation grouping |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Export | 5.569 / 6.937 | 5,738.414 / 7,067.907 | Maximum across 32 learner ranks per sync |
| NCCL send | 0.074 / 0.081 | 2,838.650 / 2,841.202 | Learner rank zero per sync |
| RPC wait | 5.367 / 5.458 | 2,612.828 / 2,688.714 | Learner rank zero per sync |
| Barrier | 6.187 / 6.454 | 6,045.054 / 6,324.449 | Maximum across 32 learner ranks per sync |
| Learner reload finalization | 0.00647 / 0.00686 | 6.493 / 6.890 | Learner rank zero per sync |
| Receive | 0.0602 / 0.0618 | Missing | Maximum receiver wall time per sync |
| Load | 4.544 / 4.630 | Missing | Maximum receiver wall time per sync |
| Receiver finalization | 0.00473 / 0.00490 | Missing | Maximum receiver wall time per sync |

All stage summaries contain five syncs. Export and barrier each have 160 underlying learner-rank observations; the other learner stages each have five. Including startup, 402 native learner stage events were retained. All 25 post-update learner wall maxima match the corresponding W&B driver metrics. Receiver wall maxima are retained in W&B, but individual receiver receipts and their CUDA times were not durably exported. The worker process returns those values over RPC without initializing a telemetry exporter.

Stage spans overlap. CUDA events can include stream waiting, while a host NCCL call can return before transfer completion; neither rank maxima nor stage medians may be summed into critical-path latency or GPU utilization.

The one-second inference polling configuration produced 2,648 cumulative token observations across eight engines. Actual sampling intervals reached 3.521 seconds. Counter differences aligned to each sync are retained with 60-second windows on either side; adjacent windows overlap other syncs and evaluation, so they do not establish a causal throughput effect. The final after-window has only 66.585% coverage and has no reported rate.

| Development evaluation | Contract score, 95% interval | Completed contract score, 95% interval | Length-stop fraction, 95% interval |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Before training | 75.00% [66.84, 81.70] | 73.44% [65.18, 80.32] | 11.72% [7.23, 18.44] |
| After five updates | 92.19% [86.22, 95.70] | 89.06% [82.48, 93.37] | 9.38% [5.44, 15.67] |

Intervals are Wilson intervals over 128 audited rows, not seed uncertainty or a paired treatment comparison. These are the retained legacy verifier and completed-stop scores; independent semantic scoring was not part of this timing gate. All 160 consumed groups have native policy-version age observations: 92 at age zero and 68 at age one. Pooled group-weighted mean age is 0.425 updates and nearest-rank p95 is one update; coverage is 32 groups per update. Behavior-ratio token-weight ESS fraction ranged from 0.991226 to 0.992424.

The separate data-loader gate failed its strict maximum-lag requirement: 373 samples included three values above two seconds, with a maximum of 2.527699 seconds. The three violations overlap weight sync; overlap does not establish their cause. The epoch reset was observed at update five, and evaluation at both required steps was verified. No lag sample reached ten seconds, but that does not satisfy the two-second criterion.

The preliminary Qwen two-GPU tests passed stage readback and the native pause precursor. Across 64 actual in-flight requests, the precursor accounted for 64 aborts and eventual completions, with zero lost requests and native first-token timestamps on every abort response. Those two tests cost 0.278617778 task H100-hours combined. They are engineering checks, not a Snowball speedup or the full repeated-sync pause gate.

**What this means.** The fixed pause and coordination spans are material optimization targets, and the whole-sync wall baseline is usable. The complete GPU-stage observability requirement remains unmet because receiver CUDA receipts were not retained. The loader change remains ungated; this five-update timing run establishes neither a quality improvement nor a recommended off-policy age range.

**Next.** Preserve receiver timing origin while exporting the native RPC receipts through the trainer, then validate the repair before a bounded Snowball rerun. Independently complete the pause-handshake checks with a matched stale-token comparison, and investigate the three lag spikes without excluding them or relaxing the threshold. These steps lead toward the telemetry and pause-fix milestone.

🤖 **Five Snowball updates stay below the event-loop lag limit**

**What we did and why.** We reran the five-update Snowball gate after the CPU profile identified
repeated tokenizer serialization as the remaining event-loop stall. The runtime changes only
omit the tokenizer from remote weight-sync client copies and repair receiver stage export.
The baseline zero-worker loader, original five-second pause grace and admission rules remain.
This is a timing mechanism test using the inherited binary GSM8K contract, not a quality-ranked
experiment. P32/I8, bf16, seed 17, C1/A1, train/dev 128/128, G4, context 8,192 and output cap
4,096 are identical to the failed trace. Eval runs at 0/5 and the fifth update crosses an epoch.

**Results.** All five updates finished, with the expected epoch reset on update five and eval at steps zero and five. Maximum event-loop lag was **1.116 seconds**, below the strict two-second limit.
All final task-window samples are retained, including 59 at step 0, 67 at step 4 and 86 at
step 5. The previous strict maximum was 2.527699240 seconds. The repaired trace contains all
546 stage events across six weight syncs, including 144 receiver events from eight distinct
origin ranks; 40 native stage max folds match W&B row by row.
Whole weight-sync p50/p95 was **17.010/17.480 seconds**, compared with 20.226/20.513 seconds in the original trace. The pause remains five seconds (repaired p50 5.235 seconds). This is a descriptive comparison of two runs; overlapping stage clocks are not additive.
The five successful east H100 task attempts cost **9.22088 task GPUh**; zero failures or
preemptions. Native terminal/runtime/request/attempt and all 256 eval rows were audited.

Eval wall times were 43.716/41.272 seconds at 0/5 versus 42.398/40.228 seconds in the failed
trace, increases of 3.11%/2.60%; total core time fell from 281.748 to 259.819 seconds. These
single-run timings do not establish a formal equivalence interval. Quality is also not

from 12/128 to 20/128. Semantic scoring was not run. The comparison conditions on these two
realized runs and does not estimate seed variability or satisfy confirmation/non-inferiority.

🤖 **A 20-update baseline fails the gate after an engine dies during startup**

**What we did and why.** We ran the original five-second-pause Qwen baseline for a matched comparison of weight-sync handshakes. The comparison requires clean operation throughout startup and training. An inference engine died during initialization, so we held the candidate and let the baseline finish to preserve its evidence.

**Results.** The baseline completed 20 updates and both evaluation dumps. Its two GPU tasks succeeded once, with no Iris retries or preemptions, costing **2.43432 task H100-hours**. Core training took 249.105 seconds and consumed 833,483 response tokens and the same number of loss tokens across 5,120 responses. Median pause was 5.027 seconds. Group-weighted mean age was 0.9 updates and pooled group p95 was 1; the consume-time token-weight ESS fraction ranged from 0.996439 to 0.998892.

The native ledger contains 1,344 completed training groups and 877,470 generated tokens, including 64 groups discarded at the epoch boundary. No completed tokens were rejected for staleness. Generated and consumed tokens have different denominators.

Initial and final completed correctness were 9/128 and 80/128, equal to raw correctness at both endpoints. Length stops increased from 1/128 to 4/128. The within-run paired-prompt improvement was 55.46875 percentage points, with conditional 95% bootstrap interval [46.875, 64.0625], 71 wins and no losses. Semantic scores were not computed.

During startup, an EngineCore failed to bind its TCPStore port with `EADDRINUSE`. The runtime retried initialization internally. That engine death **fails the whole-job gate**, despite the clean terminal training receipts. The candidate was never submitted for this pair.

**What this means.** Iris task success does not establish an error-free engine lifetime. The baseline measures the original pause but cannot qualify the matched handshake comparison. Its development-score change provides no quality-preservation or non-inferiority conclusion.

Its candidate has incomplete request-accounting receipts, so those require repair and a new qualification before accepting a pause reduction. A 16-question functional check preceded a 1,024-question pilot sampled proportionally across eight accepted training bins, with eight responses per question. Independent CPU audits checked original engine tokens, native rewards and completed correctness; the serving path also required exact agreement between API text and token decoding. We then attempted the 13,407-question remainder and a bounded 512-question diagnostic after the remainder failed that check.

**Results.**

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Functional check | 16×8 | 128 | 36,033 | 158.510 | 0.044031 | Token/reward/completion parity passed |
| Representative pilot | 1,024×8 | 8,192 | 2,068,195 | 242.926 | 0.067479 | Token/reward/completion parity passed |
| Remainder | 13,407×8 | — | — | 234.651 | 0.065181 | Renderer mismatch; no rating dump |
| Diagnostic | 512×8 | — | — | 156.638 | 0.043511 | Same check failed; offending response captured |

All four attempts used one east H100, with no automatic retries. Total measured cost is 0.220201389 H100-hours. These were inference-only jobs: training updates, off-policy age and ESS do not apply; no training-core speedup is claimed. The pilot's generation plus native scoring took 129.002900501s within its 242.926s task allocation; the functional check predates that timing instrumentation.

Pilot completed correctness was 1,909/8,192=23.30%, with a 95% question-bootstrap interval [22.19%,24.48%]. The functional prerequisite checked 256 original token hashes; the pilot checked 16,384. The functional panel was deliberately small and balanced across bins, so its answer scores are not pooled with the representative pilot.

Completed correctness is full native credit multiplied by an accepted stop. Each question contributes the mean of its eight binary outcomes. Intervals resample questions with all eight responses kept together, 10,000 draws, bootstrap seed 17; the pooled interval preserves the pilot's bin quotas. They are descriptive, pointwise intervals conditional on one engine seed, with no simultaneous-coverage, independent-seed or treatment-comparison claim. The eight-sample per-question ratings remain coarse empirical measurements, not known latent probabilities.

The pilot had 8,175 accepted stops and 17 length stops (0.2075%); all length-stopped responses had completed correctness 0. All 8,192 thinking-boundary fields were populated. Its signed/fractional raw reward mean was −0.086208839; raw values were preserved separately from binary correctness. Semantic scoring returned numeric values for 7,924 rows and left 268 unresolved (236 ambiguous, 17 conflicting, 15 unparseable). The diagnostic preserved a 67,207-byte response artifact. Replaying the exact pinned engine's incremental decoder matched the original API text for all eight responses, including the failing one; the other seven also matched whole-sequence decoding. The failed check remained strict, and neither failed attempt produced an accepted rating dump.

**What this means.**

The pilot is retained as an audited functional, cost and difficulty measurement. The full rating stage is held: a real rendering edge escaped the smaller probes, and the captured response now supplies a regression case. The correction must reproduce the engine's incremental decoding while preserving original tokens, forensic text and semantic scoring; it has not yet passed its repair gate. The initial whole-pool throughput projection is not a completed-run measurement, and these runs support no training-quality ranking or Snowball result.

**Next.**

Qualify the incremental renderer against the captured failure, EOS/stop and Unicode controls, and all 8,192 original pilot responses. Then review a fresh complete Qwen rating request on the corrected source within the remaining five-H100-hour rating budget. Snowball's native rating precursor remains held until the correction is qualified; the next milestone is the completed evaluation and task system.

🤖 3 seeded controls time out before their first recorded evaluation

**What we did and why.**

We ran a seeded control to test whether synchronous training and asynchronous training with no admitted staleness consume comparable work. This matters for attributing faster Snowball training at the same answer quality to scheduling. An earlier comparison consumed matching question sets but exceeded its prescribed reward-noise band, so the planned follow-up assigned each trajectory a seed derived from its question, sample and installed weight version and enabled the pinned engine's batch-invariance mode. The three arms were synchronous seed 17, asynchronous seed 17 and an asynchronous seed-29 noise reference, each planned for eight updates.

**Results.**

| Arm | Planned updates | Recorded training/evaluation result | Native terminal state | Task H100-hours |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Synchronous, seed 17 | 8 | No usable result | Both tasks timed out | Unavailable |
| Asynchronous, seed 17 | 8 | No usable result | Both tasks timed out | Unavailable |
| Asynchronous noise reference, seed 29 | 8 | No usable result | Both tasks timed out | Unavailable |

All six GPU tasks failed on their first attempt, with no preemption or automatic retry. Each arm requested 16 east H100s with a 1,125-second execution timeout. The controller reports execution timeout for every task, but their attempt-finish timestamps are missing. The 15-H100-hour reservation therefore remains held; it is not reported as measured cost, and the job-terminal timestamps are not substituted for allocation ends.

All three W&B runs are marked crashed with zero history rows. Independent regional storage reads found no evaluation exports, successful training receipts or terminal manifests at the exact frozen output paths. Native telemetry contains no recorded optimizer updates, training metrics or completed-work events for these runs. Consumed tokens, training-core time, completed correctness, semantic correctness, truncation, age, ESS and confidence intervals are consequently unavailable.

The runs reached receiver setup and then stopped making visible progress before initial evaluation. Source inspection shows that batch-invariance initialization changes NCCL settings in the rollout workers while the trainer retains its previous settings. That is a transport hypothesis, not a demonstrated cause: the captured stacks cover the waiting launcher, and targeted computational stacks could not be recovered before teardown. The earlier two-request determinism probe passed, but it did not exercise trainer-to-worker weight sync.

**What this means.**

This attempt does not establish synchronous/asynchronous equivalence or non-equivalence. It is a failed startup qualification with no quality comparison. The earlier reward-noise failure remains unresolved, and the seeded implementation stays isolated from the shared branch.

**Next.**

Test the exact pinned transport initialization with two GPUs and three bounded cases: original settings, receiver-only batch-invariance settings, and matching settings on both sides. Review the measured outcome before any further training attempt. The next milestone remains telemetry and the pause fix landed.

<details><summary>Provenance</summary>

Seeded sync-in-async control (K4), family `2026.09.08.92`. Frozen Marin `c81a0ea208309b328b3d7ee39ba68a6e559a2ffc` / MarinSkyRL `13a1551ccf8839d13c60a4b591af2e15f69ef6f6`. 🤖 2 transport probes leave the startup failure unresolved

**What we did and why.** We tested whether different communication settings on the trainer and rollout workers could explain the [seeded controls that timed out before training](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5587398353). Each probe used two H100s on one east-region host, the production custom process-group helper, and three fresh process groups: default settings, the pinned vLLM overrides on the receiver only, and those overrides on both processes. Deterministic payload hashes were intended to check successful weight transfer, a prerequisite for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality.

**Results.** Neither attempt produced a valid three-way comparison.

| Attempt | Default settings | Receiver-only overrides | Symmetric overrides | Task H100 hours |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| Initial | TCP rendezvous failed | TCP rendezvous failed | TCP rendezvous failed | 0.140477777778 |
| Corrected rendezvous | Port already in use | First broadcast failed in NCCL | Unknown: receipt parser failed | 0.080708888889 |

The initial launcher made every process a TCP-store client at a fresh endpoint with no server. All three cases stopped before broadcast; their receipts and cleanup were retained. A CPU reproduction through the production helper confirmed that disabling this launcher behavior allowed rendezvous and a correct collective result.

The repeat reached custom-group completion on both processes in the receiver-only case, then failed on its first 4,096-byte payload with NCCL's “received 12288 bytes instead of 512” error. Its default case failed earlier with a port collision, whose owner was not identified. The symmetric subprocess returned, but the orchestration parser raised `JSONDecodeError: Extra data` before preserving that case's outcome. Only two case receipts survived. Both attempts used one two-H100 task with no retries or preemptions. No model, dataset, training update or evaluation was involved; quality, consumed tokens, training throughput, age, ESS and confidence intervals are inapplicable.

**What this means.** The receiver-only error is an observation, not an isolated causal result: the baseline comparison is invalid and the symmetric outcome is missing. Neither probe qualifies a production communication change. A one-host transport test also cannot by itself qualify the original two-host training configuration with Ray, model loading and weight sync.

**Next.** Repair port ownership and receipt retention, including a regression for concatenated event records and preservation of raw output before parsing. Review those CPU proofs before another bounded probe. Continue correction-objective engineering independently; the next related milestone remains telemetry and the pause fix landed.

**What we did and why.** We attempted a small inference-only qualification before rating Snowball's training pool. | Tensor parallelism 8 | 8 | Model configuration rejects 20 attention heads split across eight ranks | 0.133373333333 |
| Tensor parallelism 1, data/expert parallelism 4 | 4 | Container OOM kill during model loading | 0.080462222222 |

The first CPU preparation checked architecture and context limits but missed the pinned model's parallelism restrictions. Subsequent source and native configuration checks established that its GPU implementation requires tensor parallelism one; expert parallelism provides the supported weight sharding. The second attempt reached all four intended expert ranks, each assigned 64 of the model's 256 experts, then was OOM-killed while loading. The task exited 137 after 72.416 seconds at a 128 GiB host-memory limit. No CUDA out-of-memory traceback was recorded, and peak host memory was not available in the retained task receipt.

The loader source exposes a concrete capacity mismatch: each worker defaults to a 40,000,000,000-byte CPU buffer. Four such buffers total 160 GB, exceeding the container's 137,438,953,472-byte limit before other memory use. Each worker streams the checkpoint tensors to CPU and clones them before model-specific expert selection; expert parallelism does not prevent those overlapping host allocations. This is source-backed capacity analysis, not a measurement of the failed run's peak memory.

Both attempts used one task, with no retries or preemptions. No model-load, GPU-headroom or response-rendering gate passed. Quality, tokens, core training throughput, age, ESS, truncation and confidence intervals are unavailable because no inference or learning completed.

Review an explicit 8 GiB buffer limit and concurrency four per worker, plus periodic container-memory evidence, before another bounded load probe. 🤖 40 requests remain unfinished after 13 seconds, but pause fails on request identity


**What we did and why.** Repeated the one-engine Qwen3-0.6B queue measurement with the concurrency cap reduced from eight to four. The same 64 requests, frozen east model, 1,024-token forced outputs, sampling settings, native token-space client, two measured PPO delays and original five-second grace were retained. This tested whether the smaller cap could leave work for an actual pause/abort, before spending on another full training pair.

**Results.** The native test failed before the scheduler abort: `ValueError: native frontend includes an untracked request`. The task failed with exit 1, one attempt and no retry, after 227.815 seconds, costing 0.063281944444 H100 hours against the 0.166666666667-hour ceiling. The failure occurred in the identity ledger's strict subset check at the pause boundary.

The first read spanned 4.947766–4.951584 seconds after all admissions: 56 requests were unfinished, including 52 without a first token. The second read spanned 13.137458–13.141367 seconds: 40 were unfinished, including 36 without a first token. The separate pre-grace read still saw those 40. No successful native pause was recorded. Failure cleanup returned 36 logical results and canceled 28 logical tasks; each returned result contained 1,024 tokens and finite log probabilities, totaling 36,864 completed logical tokens. Cancellation is not eventual completion.

All 36 receipt chunks were retained and independently reassembled. Through the last pre-grace snapshot, the native ledger accounts for 64 starts, 24 length terminals containing 24,576 tokens and 40 active identities. It has no post-failure native drain. Consequently, neither full emitted-token conservation nor terminal resolution of all native requests can be established from this failed run. The measured protocol lasted 18.431902 seconds. This fixture had zero learner updates and no consumed training tokens, scorer or evaluation: training throughput, off-policy age, ESS, raw/contract-completed correctness and confidence intervals are not applicable. All 36 returned outputs intentionally reached the length limit; the other 28 logical tasks were canceled.

**What this means.** The lower concurrency leaves unfinished work at both observed PPO delays, but it also exposes an interface error hidden by earlier empty pause cohorts. In the pinned engine, the frontend dictionary is keyed by randomized internal request IDs. Each `RequestState` separately preserves the external request ID passed to generation. Our ledger tracks external IDs but passed internal dictionary keys to the subset check. The old CPU fake used identical keys and external IDs, so it missed this contract. Existing native receipts did not retain raw frontend IDs, preventing a retrospective internal/external join. We will not infer that join by stripping UUID suffixes or relax the ledger check.

**Next.** Run the separately reviewed repair using the explicit external request ID and retain both identities in the pause receipt. 🤖 Eight controlled updates match training rewards across runners

### What we did and why

We compared synchronous training with the asynchronous runner restricted to zero rollout age, using Qwen3-0.6B. Both runners received the same prompt sets and request seeds, with matched communication settings before weight sync. This tests whether later comparisons can use the synchronous runner as their control (K4).

Each arm ran eight updates, with 64 prompts and four responses per prompt. We used seed 17 for the pair and seed 29 for an asynchronous repeat to measure variation. Evaluation was greedy on the same 128 development questions at startup and after training.

### Results

The seed-17 arms matched fingerprints of the consumed prompt-ID sets and raw training rewards at all eight updates. Both had zero rejected groups; the asynchronous runner consumed only age-zero rollouts. Every reward difference was therefore within the measured seed-repeat band.

Completed correctness counts answers that are correct under the task contract and finish with an accepted stop.

| Arm | Final completed correctness | Length stops | Consumed response tokens | Core training seconds | Task H100-hours |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Synchronous, seed 17 | 70/128 | 0/128 | 317,375 | 86.66 | 1.755 |
| Asynchronous, seed 17 | 68/128 | 1/128 | 317,375 | 123.90 | 1.901 |
| Asynchronous, seed 29 | 69/128 | 2/128 | 318,547 | 126.10 | 1.911 |

The full-ratio token effective-sample-size fraction ranged from 0.99875718 to 0.99901904 in both seed-17 arms and from 0.99874120 to 0.99900885 in the repeat. This measures importance-weight concentration on selected tokens.

Final asynchronous-minus-synchronous completed correctness was **−1.56 percentage points**, with a paired-question 95% interval of **[−7.03, +3.91] points**. Raw correctness equaled completed correctness at these endpoints. Semantic rescoring was unavailable for this legacy evaluation protocol.

Each seed-17 arm had one engine initialization failure caused by a port collision, followed by the runtime's built-in startup retry. All 50 observed worker processes, including failed and replacement starts, had the required settings. Scheduler retries and terminal telemetry export losses were zero. Total measured cost was 5.568 H100-hours.

### What this means

The prescribed control gate passes under these sampling and communication settings. The asynchronous runner was slower in this short, age-zero comparison. Core timing excludes startup and evaluation; this result does not rank production schedules.

The quality interval is conditional on the observed seed-17 models and is too wide to establish the 2-point non-inferiority claim. Consumed-set digests do not establish order within a batch. Earlier failed controls and the startup retries remain part of the record.

### Next

Integrate the qualified control, finish evaluation calibration, and complete the pause comparison needed for milestone 3, telemetry and pause fix landed. Quality-ranked sweeps will use the calibrated evaluation protocol.

🤖 Snowball's 256-question pilot scores 40.6% on correct, completed answers

### What we did and why

We ran four Snowball responses on each of 256 questions sampled by a frozen bin-selection rule from a 3,000-question panel that Qwen had not mastered. The pilot measures task difficulty, termination and cost before completing the larger rating panel. These ratings help select tasks for testing faster Snowball training at the same answer quality.

### Results

The task and independent artifact audit passed for all 1,024 responses. **416/1,024 (40.6%)** were correct under the task contract and finished with an accepted stop; the descriptive 95% interval is **[36.9%, 44.4%]**. Accepted stops occurred in **951/1,024 (92.9%)**, interval **[90.2%, 95.3%]**. The remaining 73 responses reached the length limit.

Percentages below include pointwise 95% intervals, resampling questions with their four responses kept together. Semantic scores use only responses the semantic scorer could resolve.

| Task bin | Questions | Correct and completed, % [CI] | Accepted stop, % [CI] | Semantic correct/resolved | Unresolved |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Arithmetic, easy | 6 | 66.7 [54.2, 83.3] | 100.0 [100.0, 100.0] | 15/15 | 9 |
| Arithmetic, medium | 13 | 36.5 [25.0, 50.0] | 100.0 [100.0, 100.0] | 40/41 | 11 |
| Arithmetic, hard | 18 | 29.2 [19.4, 38.9] | 93.1 [84.7, 100.0] | 34/44 | 28 |
| GSM8K | 110 | 55.0 [50.0, 60.0] | 98.6 [96.4, 100.0] | 334/348 | 92 |
| MATH, levels 1–2 | 27 | 38.9 [27.8, 50.0] | 98.1 [94.4, 100.0] | 78/83 | 25 |
| MATH, level 3 | 23 | 34.8 [22.8, 46.7] | 89.1 [79.3, 96.7] | 67/70 | 22 |
| MATH, level 4 | 25 | 24.0 [14.0, 34.0] | 82.0 [69.0, 93.0] | 73/75 | 25 |
| MATH, level 5 | 34 | 14.7 [8.1, 22.8] | 76.5 [64.7, 86.8] | 78/86 | 50 |

Binary contract correctness was 417/1,024; one correct response lacked an accepted stop. The raw reward mean was 0.11148, retaining signed MATH rewards and fractional arithmetic credit. It is not an accuracy percentage.

Semantic scoring found 719 correct answers among 762 resolved responses, with 262 unresolved. Among resolved responses, 412 scores disagreed with both binary contract correctness and completed correctness. No semantic-worker timeout occurred. These counts do not establish correctness for the unresolved responses.

The run produced 2,569,514 response tokens. Generation and native scoring took 1,225.12 seconds; the full task took 1,450.718 seconds on four H100s, costing **1.612 H100-hours**. Peak host memory was 66.33 GB under a 137.44 GB limit, with zero OOM events. This inference-only run has no optimizer updates, rollout age or importance-weight ESS.

### What this means

The serving and scoring path is qualified on this pilot. Contract and semantic scores disagree often enough that neither should silently replace the other. The panel was selected using Qwen's prior ratings, and these descriptive intervals do not make it an independent benchmark or certify the entire task pool.

Pilot throughput projects the remaining 2,744 questions to roughly 14.79 H100-hours using bin-specific token lengths, or 17.28 hours by scaling full task duration. Both are planning estimates; neither is a statistical upper bound.

### Next

Finish freezing the disjoint remainder request within a proposed 20-H100-hour ceiling, then complete the 3,000-question initial ratings. Fresh eight-response ratings of empirical extremes will replace their initial four-response estimates. This advances the answer-contract and task milestone; the immediate engineering milestone remains telemetry and pause fix landed.

🤖 20 pause measurements stand; final cleanup exposed a cancellation defect

**What we did and why.** We ran the original five-second-pause baseline under enough queued work to test whether a faster pause can preserve every native request. This is a stress qualification for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality (K7), using Qwen on 16 east H100s: eight learner GPUs and eight independent inference engines. Both prospective arms use 2,048 training rows, 512 generation workers, an admission-age limit of eight updates, four concurrent sequences per engine, and forced 1,024-token training responses. The candidate has not run.

**Results.**

| Arm | Updates | Consumed loss tokens | Core seconds | Task H100 hours | Final completed score | Semantic rating | Eval truncation | Consumed age mean / p95 | Token-weight ESS fraction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Original pause, failed final drain | 20 | 5,242,880 | 493.258 | 2.312793 audited for rank 0; rank 1 pending | 71/128 = 55.47%; Wilson 95% CI [46.82, 63.79]% | Not rated | 2/128 = 1.5625% | 2.202 / 7 updates | Mean 0.998550; range 0.997825–0.998854 |

All 5,120 consumed training sequences reached the forced length, and all 5,242,880 response tokens carried a loss mask. Initial raw and completed scores were both 8/128, with Wilson 95% CI [3.20, 11.85]%; final raw and completed scores were both 71/128. Initial evaluation had one length stop; final evaluation had two. These completed scores use the historical correct-answer-plus-accepted-stop definition; semantic correctness was not separately rated. No paired arm interval is available because the candidate has not yet run.

The 20 measured pauses had median 5.0999 seconds and nearest-rank p95 5.1792 seconds. Whole weight sync had median 6.2162 seconds and p95 6.3917 seconds. The audited completed-group stale-token fraction was 1,536,000 / 6,918,144 = 22.2025%, including stale-at-enqueue outcomes; this denominator excludes unfinished native work. All eight engines had real queued cohorts after the first two grace periods. Native stage coverage contains 903 events and 160 checked driver folds; per-origin CUDA durations and wall spans overlap and cannot be added into whole-sync latency.

The run then failed the frozen 30-second final idle acknowledgement. Its 3,945 request chunks reconstruct 488 receipts: initial state and all three snapshots for 20 syncs on each engine, but none of the eight required final receipts. The 29,077 native starts visible through the last recorded snapshots have matching terminal dispositions; requests resumed after those snapshots are outside that completed receipt prefix. Their final disposition is unavailable, so this is **not** a proof of whole-run conservation. W&B marks the run failed, and both the completion receipt and successful terminal manifest are absent.

The first failure was the final request-readback timeout at 19:27:09 UTC on September 8, 2026. Later metrics-endpoint connection failures occurred during teardown. Rank 0 used 1,040,757 ms on eight H100s; rank 1 is marked `cosched_failed` but still lacks a task/attempt finish timestamp. Its four-hour accounting reservation is not an observed duration or an actual-cost bound and does not delay another run. Total task cost and tokens per task H100-hour remain unresolved.

**What this means.** The workload exercises pause under a real backlog, and the final cleanup defect needs repair. The twenty measured syncs remain valid under the September 9 ruling; a final-accounting timeout after the last sync does not invalidate those measurements. A real-Ray CPU regression establishes that token-generation cancellation was not forwarded to the remote actor: the original path timed out, while routing it through the cancellation helper already used by chat stops the actor. This stress run does not establish production speedup, quality preservation, or a preferred admission-age range.

**Next.** Run the combined Snowball receiver readback and transport probe, then run the candidate with the cancellation fix and earliest first-token admission version. Keep the original baseline measurements and label the admission change when comparing the arms. Reconcile the missing task finish timestamp independently. The next milestone is completing telemetry and the pause fix (milestone 3).

🤖 Historical drift indicators do not establish a safe bound across 24 windows

**What we did and why.**

Before expanding the staleness ladder, this exploratory pilot (E4.5) tested whether existing indicators warned of the next decline in completed correctness. We reused six audited 100-update Qwen runs, all with training seed 17. Each prediction uses the preceding 20 updates and predicts the change between the current evaluation and the next one. This gives 24 dependent windows: five have a decline, and three decline by more than 2 percentage points.

The feature window, risk direction and two outcome definitions were fixed before calculating associations. Completed correctness uses the same audited verifier-plus-completed-stop endpoint as the historical reports. No new training ran. This informs the goal of faster Snowball training at the same answer quality.

**Results.**

| Indicator, fixed risk direction | AUROC: any next decline | AUROC: decline >2 pp |
|---|---:|---:|
| Lower legacy behavior-ratio ESS | 0.463 | 0.524 |
| Higher mean absolute log-ratio | 0.474 | 0.603 |
| Higher p99 absolute log-ratio | 0.442 | 0.619 |
| Higher mean squared log-ratio | 0.453 | 0.524 |
| Lower policy entropy | 0.547 | 0.619 |
| Higher raw gradient norm | 0.221 | 0.333 |
| Higher mean admitted age | 0.484 | 0.452 |

None of the available fixed-direction indicators reached AUROC 0.8 in this exploratory dataset. The whole-run bootstrap intervals are broad; for the primary endpoint, ESS is [0.159, 0.705], mean absolute log-ratio [0.206, 0.659], and low entropy [0.143, 0.798]. These intervals resample runs while retaining their dependent windows. They do not estimate variation across independent training seeds.

The existing ESS <0.5 flag never fired. A literal per-step mean-absolute-log-ratio >0.03 flag fired in two preceding windows; both were false alarms: 2/19, or 10.5%, for any subsequent decline. It missed all five declines. Applying the same threshold to each 20-update mean would erase both spikes, so that aggregation is reported separately.

The old worker absolute-log-ratio statistic is identically zero. Split stale-ratio ESS, split mismatch ESS, and gradient cosine are missing from these historical runs. In the new four-arm N1 correction screen, all 32 recorded stale-ESS values are exactly one, confirming that this particular statistic cannot discriminate rollout staleness when every batch has only one optimizer update.

All 7,800 native scalar values were recovered under exact run/job/region filters. Their 78 metric-family count/minimum/maximum/final summaries match the previous audited records in 312 checks. The pilot adds zero GPU-hours and zero optimizer updates; CPU analysis time was not separately benchmarked.

**What this means.**

The old indicators have not earned a predictive alert. The practical safe-bound rule is therefore closed for now: no predictive alert is adopted, and the ladders will be planned around the empirical quality knee. This is a design decision on the available evidence, not a universal statistical refutation. The held-out-seed AUROC ≥0.8 criterion remains untested; missing or structurally constant indicators remain untestable, not evidence of safety.

The legacy asynchronous behavior ratio combines engine mismatch and policy age. It must not be relabeled as either of the new split ratios. Type-A experiments need the actual split mismatch and age measurements; unit stale ESS in N1 is not a safe-bound signal. Health thresholds remain descriptive flags while the empirical quality knee and held-out-seed calibration determine the operating range.

**Next.**

Plan the staleness ladders around the empirical quality knee, with no predictive safe-bound alert. Keep the split-ratio and gradient-cosine telemetry and paired completed-score records so later held-out-seed evidence can reopen the rule. The next milestone is milestone 3, telemetry and pause fix landed.

<details><summary>Provenance</summary>

Historical six-arm source: the audited Qwen family `2026.09.06.16`, legacy GSM8K development battery of 128 questions, greedy evaluation at 0/20/40/60/80/100. This is an exploratory reanalysis of already observed runs, not a prospective training experiment. The historical source pairs and individual receipt URIs remain bound by `async-rl-v2-e0-audit-summary.json` and its per-run provenance; the analysis does not repin old runs.

Feature means use updates `(t−20,t]` at t=20/40/60/80; outcome is completed score at t+20 minus that at t. Startup→20 is excluded because no preceding training window exists. Risk directions are fixed; thresholds are not fitted. Whole-run bootstrap: 5,000 draws, seed 20260909; draws without both labels are omitted (4,913 valid primary draws, 4,569 sensitivity draws). The held-out-seed criterion remains untested.

Reproducible analysis: Marin analysis `fa612d1f16ae69f72042dee9b3442c9fc90dd569`, decision-wording follow-up `bb248dbade`, followed by the metadata-only operating decision in `bb248dbade`, `experiments/post_training/async_rl_indicator_audit.py`. **What we did and why.** We finished four-response Snowball ratings on the frozen 3,000-question panel selected from questions Qwen had not mastered, combining the audited pilot with its disjoint remainder. The difficulty-rating study (KE7) helps choose tasks for testing faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. Completed correctness means the task verifier awards full credit and the response has an accepted stop.

**Results.** Across 12,000 responses, 4,829 were correct and completed: **40.24%, descriptive 95% interval [39.10%, 41.37%]**. Accepted stops occurred in 10,995 responses (91.63%); 1,005 reached the length limit. **What we did and why.** We measured evaluation and training-seed variation
before using small-model experiments to choose faster Snowball training at

frozen 1,918-question training view, then exported actual checkpoint weights.
Each checkpoint received five greedy passes on 256 development questions,
a separate greedy heldout pass, and separate stochastic panels with one,
four and eight draws on all 2,009 heldout questions.

**Results.**

| Anchor training seed | Heldout K8 completed | Pointwise 95% interval | Semantic correct / resolved | Semantic unresolved | Contract–semantic disagreements | Dev questions changing across five greedy passes |

The paired difference is 8.61 percentage points, with a pointwise interval
of 7.56–9.65 points. These are large-question normal intervals conditional on
these two trained checkpoints, with each question's eight responses kept
together. They do not cover uncertainty over future training seeds.
The Platinum component contributes 2,606 versus 4,087 completed responses
out of 9,672; the MATH component contributes 4,236 versus 4,138 out of 6,400.

All 58,812 response rows across the two checkpoints passed exact native
token, request, renderer and contract-metric audits. Training, export and
calibration used 14.53 task H100-hours combined; evaluation alone used 0.635.

The balanced seed-by-question decomposition on the stochastic eight-draw
panel gives variance components 0.003688 for training seed, 0.112529 for
question, 0.013637 for their interaction and 0.121076 for draw residuals.
All raw estimates are positive. Seed variance has only one degree of freedom.

Under the explicit assumption that those marginal components apply equally
to two future arms, two training seeds and 2,009 questions with eight draws
give the following endpoint MDE planning sensitivity for the prespecified
45-contrast correction family, at 80% power and two-sided familywise 5% error:

| Assumed correlation of each component between future arms | Planning MDE |
| --- | ---: |
| −1 | 35.83 pp |
| 0, primary assumption | 25.34 pp |
| 0.5 | 17.92 pp |
| 0.9 | 8.01 pp |

The full artifact retains every componentwise correlation combination,
all raw and truncated moments, and the smaller prespecified comparison
families. These are normal planning approximations, not certified power
or confidence limits on the MDE. The endpoint calculation does not establish
power for a four-arm difference in age degradation.

**What this means.** The earlier rough five-point MDE is not supported by this
calibration under the stated assumptions. Similar development scores did
not predict heldout contract stability; the near-equal semantic totals and

The two-seed estimate is too uncertain to certify a two-point non-inferiority

perturbation seeds to measure paired differences under its actual runner and

The calibration and indicator results make the confirmation work essential: uncertainty must be measured across training seeds, and constant or missing indicators cannot certify safety.

**Next.** Complete the fresh Snowball ratings and disagreement review, finish the reuse-ladder evaluations, and qualify receiver readback and inter-host transport for the next weight-sync improvements. The next milestone is **4, answer contract and tasks fixed**.
