spillover_issues.title: [marin] Replace assert validation and narrow swallowed failures

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
# Slop Audit: Marin, Levanter, Haliax, and Tests

Audit date: 2026-06-16  
Commit reviewed: [`000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f)  
Scope: `lib/marin`, `lib/levanter`, `lib/haliax`, and all `tests`, excluding `experiments` implementation files. Tests that import `experiments` were still reviewed because the request included all tests.

## Taxonomy

| ID | Slop Type | Signal | Why It Is Negative |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S1 | Behaviorless tests | No assertion or only "does not raise" smoke coverage. | The test can pass while the behavior is wrong, and often only proves that imports/config wiring happened once. |
| S2 | Tautological tests | `isinstance`, registry membership, constructor/default checks, `is not None`, "method exists". | These mostly prove Python, dataclasses, or global registration, not user-visible behavior. |
| S3 | Implementation-pinned tests | Assertions on `_private` fields/helpers, call counts, internal dispatch, exact helper order. | They fail under harmless refactors and miss externally visible regressions. |
| S4 | Brittle timing/infrastructure tests | `time.sleep`, real network/GCS/HF dependencies in unit-shaped tests, manual benchmark tests. | They are flaky, slow, skipped in CI, or environment-dependent instead of behavior-dependent. |
| S5 | Permanent skip graveyard | `@pytest.mark.skip` without a path to re-enable. | Dead tests look like coverage while providing none. This is explicitly rejected by `TESTING.md`. |
| S6 | Swallowed failure paths | Broad `except Exception: pass`, `return None`, or `return False` with little/no context. | Real bugs become silent fallbacks; operators lose the cause of production failures. |
| S7 | Assert-as-validation | `assert` used for runtime input validation or externally reachable errors. | Assertions disappear under optimized Python and conflate invariants with user/config errors. |
| S8 | Weak boundary contracts | Tests mock inside the system instead of using a fake boundary or persisted state. | They verify wiring rather than effects and tend to bless the current implementation shape. |

Severity rubric:

| Rating | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| High | Masks real failures, creates false confidence in critical code, or removes coverage entirely. |
| Medium | Brittle or low-value enough to slow refactors and reviews, but some behavior signal remains. |
| Low | Local cleanup; not harmful alone, but part of a repeated pattern. |

## Findings

### 1. Permanent skipped tests and manual benchmarks are acting as fake coverage

Rating: High  
Taxonomy: S4, S5

Representative sources:

- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_train_asr.py:16`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_train_asr.py#L16)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/whisper_test.py:28`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/whisper_test.py#L28)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_attention.py:64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_attention.py#L64)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_audio.py:57`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_audio.py#L57) and [`test_audio.py:110`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_audio.py#L110)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_hf_gpt2_serialize.py:50`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_hf_gpt2_serialize.py#L50)
- [`tests/rl/test_weight_transfer.py:293`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/rl/test_weight_transfer.py#L293) and [`test_weight_transfer.py:377`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/rl/test_weight_transfer.py#L377)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_gdn_kernels.py:471`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_gdn_kernels.py#L471)

These are not normal conditional skips such as optional-dependency or backend gating. Several are permanently disabled with TODO/flaky/gone-file reasons, or are benchmark/manual tests checked into pytest collection. Delete them, move manual benchmarks out of pytest, or mark them with a real runnable condition plus behavior assertions.

### 2. Large smoke tests have no behavioral contract

Rating: High for training/export entrypoints; Medium for tracker wrappers  
Taxonomy: S1, S6

Representative sources:

- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_train_lm.py:31`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_train_lm.py#L31)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_train_lm.py:57`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_train_lm.py#L57)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_viz_lm.py:19`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_viz_lm.py#L19)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_export_to_hf.py:23`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_export_to_hf.py#L23)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_trackio.py:15`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_trackio.py#L15)
- [`tests/vllm/test_llm_inference.py:33`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/vllm/test_llm_inference.py#L33)

The comments say "just testing if ... has a pulse"; the tests then run expensive code without checking a stable effect. Some also swallow cleanup failures with `except Exception: pass`. Better contracts would check checkpoint files, exported HF config/loadability, generated visualization artifacts, logged records, or a small structured result.

### 3. Private representation tests are overfitting current internals

Rating: Medium  
Taxonomy: S3

Representative sources:

- [`lib/haliax/tests/test_named_ref.py:82`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/haliax/tests/test_named_ref.py#L82)
- [`lib/haliax/tests/test_named_ref.py:91`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/haliax/tests/test_named_ref.py#L91)
- [`lib/haliax/tests/test_named_ref.py:169`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/haliax/tests/test_named_ref.py#L169)
- [`lib/haliax/tests/test_named_ref.py:214`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/haliax/tests/test_named_ref.py#L214)
- [`tests/execution/test_artifact_registry.py:155`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/execution/test_artifact_registry.py#L155)
- [`tests/execution/test_artifact_registry.py:259`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/execution/test_artifact_registry.py#L259)
- [`tests/rl/test_replay_buffer.py:464`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/rl/test_replay_buffer.py#L464)

`NamedRef` already has good observable tests around value reads/writes and axes. The `_prefix`/`_ref` checks pin the internal slice encoding. The artifact registry checks similarly assert `_root` rather than behavior through a public property or lookup. If the representation is truly part of the contract, expose a named public inspection API; otherwise test public behavior.

### 4. Registry and type-only tests provide weak signal

Rating: Medium  
Taxonomy: S2

Representative sources:

- [`tests/evals/test_structured_evals.py:7`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/evals/test_structured_evals.py#L7)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_tracker.py:23`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_tracker.py#L23)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_tracker.py:29`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_tracker.py#L29)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py:356`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py#L356)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py:407`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py#L407)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py:429`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py#L429)

`TESTING.md` explicitly calls registration tests slop. Membership in an eval set or a draccus choice registry may be useful as a config smoke probe, but it is not behavior coverage. Prefer a tiny end-to-end decode/stage/run through the public boundary, or collapse these into one explicit schema/config contract test with stronger assertions.

### 5. Mock-dispatch tests verify helper wiring instead of effects

Rating: Medium  
Taxonomy: S3, S8

Representative sources:

- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py:1474`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py#L1474)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py:1492`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py#L1492)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py:1509`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py#L1509)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py:1525`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/test_tokenizers.py#L1525)
- [`lib/haliax/tests/test_ragged_dot_dispatch.py:60`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/haliax/tests/test_ragged_dot_dispatch.py#L60)
- [`lib/levanter/tests/kernels/test_pallas_fused_cross_entropy_loss.py:1118`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/levanter/tests/kernels/test_pallas_fused_cross_entropy_loss.py#L1118)

The tokenizer staging tests are the clearest cases: several assertions are `assert_not_called()` / `assert_called_once()` on private staging helpers. They should assert final staged files, cache reuse, corrupt mirror recovery, and no network boundary hit through a fake external boundary. Some kernel dispatch tests do assert output/warnings too, so they are less bad, but the call-count assertions should remain secondary to observable fallback behavior.

### 6. Sleep-based tests encode timing races

Rating: Medium  
Taxonomy: S4

Representative sources:

- [`tests/rl/test_replay_buffer.py:140`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/rl/test_replay_buffer.py#L140)
- [`tests/rl/test_rollout_storage.py:124`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/rl/test_rollout_storage.py#L124)
- [`tests/rl/integration/test_weight_sync.py:64`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/rl/integration/test_weight_sync.py#L64)
- [`tests/rl/integration/test_rollout_worker.py:61`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/rl/integration/test_rollout_worker.py#L61)
- [`tests/integration/iris/test_iris_integration.py:129`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/integration/iris/test_iris_integration.py#L129)

Root `TESTING.md` says not to use `time.sleep()` in tests. Use fake clocks, injected timestamp sources, poll-with-deadline helpers, or event synchronization. `test_rollout_storage` is especially fixable: timestamp ordering can use an injected `now` or explicit sortable metadata instead of sleeping 10ms.

### 7. Runtime validation uses `assert`

Rating: High  
Taxonomy: S7

Representative sources:

- [`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/inference_ctx/render.py:202`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/inference_ctx/render.py#L202)
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/inference_ctx/render.py:277`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/inference_ctx/render.py#L277)
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/inference_ctx/render.py:326`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/environments/inference_ctx/render.py#L326)

These are externally reachable renderer/tokenizer conditions, not internal proofs. Under `python -O`, they disappear. Replace them with explicit `ValueError`/domain exceptions carrying the role/model/tokenizer context.

### 8. Best-effort production paths swallow broad failures

Rating: Medium to High depending on path  
Taxonomy: S6

Representative sources:

- [`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/rollout_worker.py:617`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/rollout_worker.py#L617)
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/rl/weight_transfer/arrow_flight.py:84`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/weight_transfer/arrow_flight.py#L84)
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/transform/conversation/transform_conversation.py:111`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/marin/src/marin/transform/conversation/transform_conversation.py#L111)
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/evalchemy_evaluator.py:91`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/evalchemy_evaluator.py#L91)
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/evalchemy_evaluator.py:250`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evaluators/evalchemy_evaluator.py#L250)
- [`lib/marin/src/marin/execution/executor.py:318`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/lib/marin/src/marin/execution/executor.py#L318)

Some of these are intentionally best-effort, but the implementation pattern is still sloppy: broad catches with no structured signal. Catch expected exception types, log at debug/warning with context, increment a metric when applicable, and keep the fallback explicit. For parser normalization, decide whether invalid JSON arguments should remain raw, become an error, or be tagged as unparsed.

### 9. Real-service and hard-coded-path tests blur unit/integration boundaries

Rating: Medium  
Taxonomy: S4

Representative sources:

- [`tests/vllm/test_llm_inference.py:35`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/vllm/test_llm_inference.py#L35)
- [`tests/rl/test_checkpoint_transfer.py:20`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/rl/test_checkpoint_transfer.py#L20)
- [`tests/rl/test_checkpoint_transfer.py:28`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/rl/test_checkpoint_transfer.py#L28)
- [`tests/rl/test_rl_experiment_utils.py:158`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/000aff1b3894df6ae78642b0e71c49a020aecd8f/tests/rl/test_rl_experiment_utils.py#L158)

Tests with real GCS model paths, CI-wide skips, or TPU-only service assumptions should be clearly integration-marked and separated from unit tests. Where possible, use temp fsspec filesystems or existing fakes to check path reconstruction and region behavior.

## Not Flagged Despite Pattern Matches

- `np.testing.*` assertions were initially detected as "no assert" by AST because they are function calls. I treated those as real assertions.
- Exact string checks in data rendering tests often are real contracts because downstream readers consume rendered text/JSONL. I did not flag those unless they were only incidental logs/messages.
- Some background/concurrency tests use private helpers such as `_wait_until_idle`; those still assert observable forwarded logs/artifacts, so I did not treat the helper use alone as a finding. The private queue/drop counter assertion is weaker but not as severe as the representation-pinned tests.

## Recommended Cleanup Order

1. Delete or re-home permanent skips/manual benchmarks. This removes fake coverage quickly.
2. Add explicit artifacts/output assertions to Levanter entrypoint smoke tests (`train_lm`, `viz_lm`, export, Trackio).
3. Replace `assert` runtime validation in Marin renderers with explicit exceptions and tests for those exceptions.
4. Refactor the highest-churn private representation tests (`NamedRef`, artifact registry) toward public behavior contracts.
5. Replace sleep-based RL/storage tests with fake clocks or poll/event synchronization.
6. Narrow broad production catches and add structured logging/metrics for intentional best-effort fallbacks.

## Scan Method

I reviewed repository guidance (`AGENTS.md`, `TESTING.md`, and subproject `AGENTS.md` files), then scanned 824 Python files in scope with `rg` and an AST probe for:

- no-assert test functions,
- `isinstance`/`hasattr`/`is None`/`is not None` assertions,
- private attribute assertions,
- mock call assertions,
- broad `pytest.raises`,
- `time.sleep`,
- `pytest.mark.skip`,
- broad `except` handlers that pass or return sentinel values,
- hard-coded `gs://marin...` paths and environment-dependent test setup.

I manually inspected representative hits before assigning ratings.

spillover_issues.title: [slop] Audit Marin, Levanter, Haliax, and tests

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
Our current grug/pipeline examples all require the user to initiate them via the `uv run iris` command line. This introduces an easy place to accumulate errors:

* Should the user have passed a reservation, but forgot?
* Did they ask for resources the script didn't need, thinking it needed to run the launcher on a TPU
* Did they put it in the wrong region?

This adds up to wasted time and energy. Let's adjust all of our boot scripts to instead hoist the Iris client themselves, and incorporate any CLI options _they_ want to specify e.g. region, or TPU type. We can apply a common pattern, but we don't need a marin launcher library or anything.

Let's add a warning if they are run and e.g. `iris.job_info()` is not None: this indicates the user accidentally ran them from the `uv run iris` command instead of directly.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Plan:**
- [x] Read AGENTS.md + fix-issue/commit skills
- [x] Actionability check — actionable (clear definition of done)
- [x] Duplicate-work preflight — no open PR/issue
- [x] Research current launch pattern + Iris client SDK
- [x] Scope assessment — multi-script design change (>100 LOC, multi-module) → analysis, not PR
- [ ] Human review of proposed approach before implementation

# Research

Boot scripts (`experiments/grug/*`, `experiments/tutorials/*`, ~13 files) end with an `if __name__ == "__main__"` block that calls a submit helper relying on `current_client()`. `current_client()` only reaches the cluster when the script is *already inside* an Iris task — i.e. when launched via `uv run iris --cluster=marin job run -- python -m experiments.grug.base.launch`. Run plainly (`python launch.py`) it silently falls back to `LocalClient`. So the cluster/region/resources/extras live in the hand-typed `iris job run` line, not in the script — exactly the error surface the issue calls out (forgotten reservation, wrong region, over-requested launcher resources).

All the machinery to connect from a dev box (resolve cluster name → config → controller discovery → tunnel → stored token → `IrisClient`) already exists, but it is embedded in the **click CLI**, not exposed as a callable SDK entry point. Making scripts self-running means extracting that into a reusable helper and rewriting every boot script's `__main__`.

**Relevant code**
- [`experiments/grug/base/launch.py#L251-L252`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/base/launch.py#L251-L252) — current `__main__`, no client hoist
- [`experiments/defaults.py#L375-L408`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/defaults.py#L375-L408) — `_submit_train_job` → `current_client()`
- [`experiments/grug/dispatch.py#L42-L62`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/dispatch.py#L42-L62) — closest existing direct-submit pattern
- [`lib/iris/src/iris/cli/connect.py#L83-L129`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/connect.py#L83-L129) — controller discovery + tunnel (to extract)
- [`lib/iris/src/iris/cli/main.py#L112-L155`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/main.py#L112-L155) — cluster→config + token resolution
- [`lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/client/job_info.py#L85`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/client/job_info.py#L85) — `get_job_info()` for the misuse warning

# Proposed Approach (design change — review before implementation)

Multi-module and >100 LOC, so flagging for review rather than opening a PR.

**1. Expose connection as an SDK helper (no new "launcher library").** Extract the non-click parts of `connect.py`/`main.py` into a callable, e.g. `iris.client.connect_cluster(cluster: str, *, timeout_ms=...) -> IrisClient` that resolves the cluster config via `resolve_cluster_config`, discovers the controller, establishes the tunnel (returned as a context manager so it closes cleanly), loads the stored `iris login` token, and returns a connected `IrisClient`. The CLI then calls the same helper, so there is one connection path, not two.

**2. Add a small shared `__main__` helper for experiments** (e.g. `experiments/launch.py` or extend `experiments/defaults.py`) that:
   - parses CLI options with the repo's existing `draccus` pattern: `--cluster` (default `marin`), `--region`, `--tpu-type` — overriding the script's `ResourceConfig`/region instead of requiring an `iris job run` line;
   - **warns on misuse**: if `get_job_info() is not None`, the script was launched *via* `uv run iris` (double-wrapping) — log a prominent warning per the issue (open question below: warn-and-continue vs hard-fail);
   - hoists the client via `connect_cluster(...)`, sets it as the current Fray client (`set_current_client`), then runs the script's existing submit path unchanged (`_submit_train_job`/`dispatch_grug_training_run` already go through `current_client()`).

**3. Convert the ~13 boot scripts** to call this helper from `__main__`, and update `experiments/grug/README.md` + tutorial docs to drop the `uv run iris job run` invocation in favor of `uv run python experiments/grug/base/launch.py --cluster=marin --tpu-type=v5p-8`.

**Open questions for a human**
- Where should the extracted connection helper live — `iris.client` (preferred; keeps cluster-resolution in Iris) vs `fray`?
- On accidental in-job execution (`get_job_info() is not None`): warn-and-continue, or hard-fail? The issue says "add a warning," so warn-and-continue unless you prefer a fail.
- Resources today come from each script's `ResourceConfig` (e.g. `ResourceConfig.with_tpu("v5p-8")`). `--tpu-type`/`--region` should override these — confirm precedence (CLI > script default).

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This issue scopes a tokenizer-sensitivity experiment for small MoE training: hold the MoE ladder and training budget fixed, retokenize Rav's datakit testbed with several tokenizers, and compare training/eval behavior before deciding whether deeper tokenizer work is worth prioritizing. The current conclusion is that the full proposal is still a multi-phase research effort, but the smallest useful first slice is clear: pin the `data/datakit/sample/2026-05-18` testbed artifact, choose one MoE ladder size and token budget, run a few HF-loadable tokenizer arms such as Llama-3, GPT-2, and Gemma-3, freeze Paloma plus Uncheatable as the first eval suite, and defer TokenMonster plus trained-tokenizer cascades until those design choices are pinned.

### Helpful links
- Agent triage with proposed first slice and blockers: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5821#issuecomment-4482895293
- Testbed artifact pointer: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5821#issuecomment-4521984281
- Tokenizer roadmap parent: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4971
- Raw perplexity gap reports: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4934
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

We want to understand whether tokenizer choice materially changes small-scale MoE training outcomes in Marin. This issue is an experimental branch of the tokenizer roadmap: instead of deciding tokenizer design up front, it asks whether tokenizer choice moves training and eval behavior enough to justify deeper work.

From the weekly modeling discussion, tokenization is a self-contained axis that could affect model quality, per-domain behavior, and multilingual performance. A useful first pass is to add another tokenizer family, such as TokenMonster, retokenize Rav's testbed dataset several ways, train a small MoE ladder, and compare losses and evals.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Measure how sensitive our MoE setup is to tokenizer choice.

If TokenMonster or another tokenizer has a substantially different profile across domains, languages, or evals, tokenization is probably worth prioritizing. If results are broadly flat, deeper tokenizer work can stay lower priority.

### Links

* TokenMonster paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.20757
* Tokenizer roadmap: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4971
* Number tokenization: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4915
* Tokenizer comparison for whitespace-sensitive long-tail PPL slices: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5079
* Raw perplexity gap reports: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4934

## Proposed work

### Phase 1: Compare existing tokenizers

* Find and document Rav's testbed dataset artifact.
* Retokenize the testbed with `K` tokenizers, including the current Marin baseline (aka llama3.1) tokenizer, TokenMonster, qwen3, and maybe another one or two others (gemma, gpt-oss?).
* Train a small MoE ladder on each tokenized version, probably similar to the moe agent experiments.
* Keep the model/training setup fixed except for tokenizer-dependent quantities. Still track model flops.
* Track tokenizer name/version, vocab size, dataset artifact, token counts by domain/language, training config, eval config, and run links.

### Phase 2: Analyze behavior

Compare tokenizers on training loss, validation loss, per-domain loss, per-language loss, Paloma, Uncheatable, the new PPL evals once landed, and any notable differences in token count, compression ratio, or domain/language skew.

Write up an opinionated conclusion: did tokenizer choice matter at this scale, did any tokenizer improve average performance, did any tokenizer change the profile across domains/languages, and are the differences large enough to justify more tokenizer work?

### Phase 3: Train tokenizer cascade

In parallel or after Phase 1 starts:

* Take a ~1% subsample of the testbed dataset.
* Overweight smaller domains so the tokenizer training mix does not get dominated by the largest sources.
* Train a cascade of tokenizers with approximate vocab sizes 8K, 64K, and 128K.
* Retokenize the testbed with these trained tokenizers.
* Repeat the same small MoE ladder and eval suite.
* Compare against the baseline tokenizer and off-the-shelf tokenizer results.

## Results

Updated May 26, 2026:

* W&B report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Tokenizer-Sensitivity-MoE-Ladder-d512-d768-d1024--VmlldzoxNzAxMDY2OA
* Use BPB as the primary cross-tokenizer comparison metric; token-level losses are not directly comparable when tokenizers change.
* d512 and d768 completed across all six tokenizer arms. d1024 is not fully complete: 5/6 arms finished, while `marin-128k` failed after logging an eval at step 4000 / 12648.
* d512 final eval macro BPB: `tokenmonster-englishcode-32k` 1.2689, `llama3-128k` 1.3114, `gemma3-262k` 1.3123, `marin-128k` 1.3136, `gpt-oss-200k` 1.3138, `qwen3-152k` 1.3188.
* d768 final eval macro BPB: `tokenmonster-englishcode-32k` 1.1310, `gpt-oss-200k` 1.1623, `gemma3-262k` 1.1627, `llama3-128k` 1.1693, `marin-128k` 1.1706, `qwen3-152k` 1.1712.

Current readout: TokenMonster is consistently best on aggregate BPB at d512, d768, and among finished d1024 arms, but it has worse token-level macro loss because token-level losses are tokenizer-dependent. Before closing the experiment, decide whether to rerun the failed d1024 `marin-128k` baseline and add the requested per-domain/per-language analysis.

## Acceptance criteria

* Rav's testbed dataset is identified and linked.
* Baseline tokenizer results are recorded.
* At least one meaningfully different tokenizer, preferably TokenMonster, is evaluated.
* Small MoE ladder runs complete for each tokenizer variant.
* Per-domain and per-language loss analysis is included.
* Paloma, Uncheatable, and available new PPL evals are included.
* Trained tokenizer cascade at ~8K, ~64K, and ~128K vocab sizes is evaluated, unless blocked and documented.
* Final writeup gives a clear recommendation.

## Open questions

* What exact `K` tokenizers should be included in the first pass?
* Which MoE ladder configs should be used?
* Where is Rav's latest testbed dataset artifact?
* Which new PPL evals should be considered landed enough for this comparison?
* Should tokenizer training optimize for document mix, byte coverage, language balance, or compression ratio?

🤖 Update on the tokenizer-sensitivity follow-ups:

I addressed the three open questions from the recent comments:

1. `marin-128k` is the `marin-community/marin-tokenizer` arm from the earlier matrix. Going forward I would not treat it as the 128k baseline for this issue; I used `llama3-128k` (`meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B`) as the baseline for the d1024 gap evals and skipped the unfinished `marin-128k` arm.
2. TokenMonster BPB accounting was patched for token types / capcode-shift behavior / byte fallback.
3. d1024 perplexity score + gap evals were run for the finished arms against `llama3-128k`.

Experiment page:
https://marin.community/data-browser/experiment?path=gs%3A//marin-eu-west4/experiments/exp_tokenizer_sensitivity_d1024_perplexity_gap-c91f6c.json

### Patched d1024 score summary

Lower BPB is better. The “overall” column is byte-weighted over the evaluated dataset groups.

| tokenizer | overall BPB | Paloma BPB | Uncheatable BPB |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `llama3-128k` | 0.94288 | 0.98032 | 0.85852 |
| `qwen3-152k` | 0.94321 | 0.97992 | 0.86048 |
| `gemma3-262k` | 0.93881 | 0.97767 | 0.85123 |
| `gpt-oss-200k` | 0.93911 | 0.97737 | 0.85289 |
| `tokenmonster-englishcode-32k` | 0.95095 | 0.98886 | 0.86551 |

### Patched d1024 gap vs `llama3-128k`

Gap is `candidate - llama3-128k`, so negative is better than `llama3-128k`.

| tokenizer | overall gap BPB | Paloma gap BPB | Uncheatable gap BPB | readout |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `qwen3-152k` | +0.00033 | -0.00040 | +0.00196 | basically tied / slight overall worse |
| `gemma3-262k` | -0.00408 | -0.00265 | -0.00729 | best overall in this eval |
| `gpt-oss-200k` | -0.00377 | -0.00295 | -0.00562 | close second |
| `tokenmonster-englishcode-32k` | +0.00807 | +0.00854 | +0.00700 | worse overall after the patch |

Notable per-dataset deltas:

| tokenizer | examples |
|---|---|
| `qwen3-152k` | better on `paloma/4chan` (-0.01274) and `paloma/c4_en` (-0.00209), worse on GitHub Python (+0.00997) and C++ (+0.00844) |
| `gemma3-262k` | strongest code deltas: GitHub Python -0.01823, C++ -0.02365; also better Paloma overall |
| `gpt-oss-200k` | broad improvement; GitHub Python -0.01315, C++ -0.01318 |
| `tokenmonster-englishcode-32k` | better on code-ish slices such as `paloma/dolma_100_programing_languages` (-0.01206) and GitHub C++ (-0.01311), but worse on ordinary text slices such as `paloma/c4_en` (+0.01773) and `uncheatable_eval/wikipedia_english` (+0.01201) |

### What changed in TokenMonster byte accounting

Old behavior:

- The generic BPB path assumed an HF-like tokenizer where a token’s byte contribution can be inferred from token text / decode behavior.
- That is not safe for TokenMonster because raw TokenMonster tokens can include capcode / shift / control markers that are not source-text bytes.
- Prefix underscore / byte fallback can also distort accounting if the raw token representation is treated as text. In particular, fallback replacement glyphs and control markers can make the denominator disagree with the original document bytes.
- The running BPB mean was also being accumulated with token/loss weights rather than byte weights, which is the wrong aggregation when comparing tokenizers.

New behavior:

- Added a TokenMonster tokenizer backend for this eval path.
- TokenMonster byte length uses `id_to_token_decoded` and dictionary token type metadata instead of raw token strings.
- Special/control tokens count as 0 source bytes.
- Byte fallback ids count as source bytes, not as the UTF-8 length of the replacement character.
- Delete-space markers are handled as a negative byte adjustment against the next decoded token.
- Per-token byte spans are produced against the original source UTF-8 bytes, including normalization/remapping for cases where TokenMonster decodes to a normalized Unicode form.
- The raw perplexity-gap scorer now accepts tokenizer-provided byte offsets, so TokenMonster no longer needs a fake HF fast-tokenizer offset path.
- BPB aggregation is byte-weighted.

So the earlier d1024 W&B readout where `tokenmonster-englishcode-32k` looked best among finished arms should be treated as superseded for TokenMonster interpretation. With the patched raw-score/gap path, TokenMonster is not the best d1024 arm; `gemma3-262k` and `gpt-oss-200k` are better than `llama3-128k`, while TokenMonster is worse overall but still has favorable deltas on some code-like slices.

Caveat: this is still not a pure intrinsic-tokenizer-quality comparison. The larger-vocab tokenizers (`gemma3-262k`, `gpt-oss-200k`, `qwen3-152k`) have larger embedding / LM-head parameter counts at fixed `d_model`, and a fixed token budget can correspond to different numbers of raw bytes seen. BPB fixes the eval denominator, but it does not by itself control those training/setup effects.

- Scores: `gs://marin-eu-west4/analysis/model_perplexity_scores/tokenizer-sensitivity-d1024/`
- Gaps: `gs://marin-eu-west4/analysis/perplexity_gap/tokenizer-sensitivity-d1024/`

- [From Digits to Decisions: How Tokenization Impacts Arithmetic in LLMs](https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/number-tokenization-blog)
- [Arcee Trinity Large Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.17004v1#S2) Section 2.1.1 notes a standard regex has pathological backtracking behavior and details their fix.

comments.author: pc0618
pc0618
comments.body:
## Numeric-aware tokenizer variant update

The `*-place-digits` variants currently differ from their corresponding normal `gpt-oss` / `llama` variants only in numeric pretokenization before BPE training.

The three numeric-specific changes are:

1. **Digit-run isolation**: contiguous Unicode numeric runs are separated from surrounding text before the normal tokenizer pretokenizer runs. Example: `abc1234567def` is handled as `abc | 1234567 | def` before numeric chunking.
2. **Right-to-left, place-aligned 3-digit grouping**: each digit run is split from the right into groups of three, with a leading group of one or two digits if needed. Example: `1234567 -> 1 | 234 | 567`. This keeps each 3-digit token aligned to a fixed place-value block.
3. **Bounded, backtracking-safe implementation**: instead of one zero-width lookahead over arbitrary-length digit strings, the implementation caps numeric-run chunks at 510 characters, peels a leading 1-2 digit group when needed, then splits exact groups of 3. This preserves the intended place-aligned split for normal numeric runs and avoids pathological regex backtracking on very long digit strings.

Implementation reference in this branch:

- `experiments/datakit_testbed/tokenizer_sweep_20260526.py`
- `tests/datakit_testbed/test_tokenizer_sweep_20260526.py`

Paper/source rationale:

- Singh & Strouse (2024), **"Tokenization counts: the impact of tokenization on arithmetic in frontier LLMs"**: motivates right-to-left numeric grouping; they find right-to-left number tokenization substantially improves arithmetic behavior. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14903
- Schmidt, Reddy, Tanner & Pinter (2025), **"Boundless Byte Pair Encoding: Breaking the Pre-tokenization Barrier"**: uses right-to-left 3-digit numeric pretokens and gives the same `1234567 -> [1, 234, 567]` behavior. https://arxiv.org/html/2504.00178v2

Latest preliminary tokenizer-MoE validation results show the numeric-aware variants are useful for `gpt-oss`, especially at d768:

| comparison | vocab | dim | baseline all BPB | digits all BPB | delta |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| gpt-oss -> gpt-oss-place-digits | 8k | d512 | 1.4006 | 1.3525 | -0.0481 |
| gpt-oss -> gpt-oss-place-digits | 8k | d768 | 1.1432 | 1.1134 | -0.0298 |
| gpt-oss -> gpt-oss-place-digits | 32k | d512 | 1.4418 | 1.3652 | -0.0766 |
| gpt-oss -> gpt-oss-place-digits | 32k | d768 | 1.1705 | 1.1051 | -0.0654 |
| llama -> llama-place-digits | 8k | d512 | 1.4729 | 1.4852 | +0.0123 |
| llama -> llama-place-digits | 8k | d768 | 1.2196 | 1.2203 | +0.0007 |
| llama -> llama-place-digits | 32k | d512 | 1.4656 | 1.4277 | -0.0379 |
| llama -> llama-place-digits | 32k | d768 | 1.2076 | 1.1751 | -0.0325 |

Interpretation: this is a promising signal for explicit numeric pretokenization, especially for GPT-OSS-family tokenizers and 32k vocabularies. The 8k Llama-family result is neutral/slightly worse in this preliminary train50B tokenizer-MoE table, so we should keep the numeric-aware arm as an explicit sibling variant rather than silently replacing the default tokenizer.

spillover_issues.author: Helw150
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

The mixture swap projects **1.07× macro compute-equivalent speedup at d1536** over the old ladder in #8435. This forecasts final BPB from evaluations through 80% of training, with the smaller-run backtest adjustment. The d512 mixture-search swarm gives **1.17× macro speedup**, estimated from measured final BPB across three seeds per mix.

| Paloma evaluation | d1536 adjusted forecast | d512 swarm estimate |
|---|---:|---:|
| **Macro** | **1.07×** | **1.17×** |
| Code: 100 programming languages | **1.08×** | **1.70×** |
| Academic documents: M2D2 S2ORC | 1.13× | 1.13× |
| Falcon RefinedWeb | 1.08× | 1.10× |
| Dolma v1.5 | 1.09× | 1.16× |

All speedups use BPB and assume equal throughput. Swarm estimates transfer the old ladder’s scaling slopes to d512; they are not measured runtime savings. The swarm helped select this mix and switches after 10% of training, versus 25% in this ladder.

The swarm also measures **1.43% lower mean Uncheatable BPB**, including **5.11% lower on C++** and **2.09% lower on Python**. The old scaling ladder has no Uncheatable baseline, so we cannot fit an Uncheatable speedup curve. Swarm methods and source data are below.

Completed d768/d1024 runs improve macro BPB by 0.41%/0.70%, but code BPB regresses at both widths. The d768 lead predates the switch. Academic-document forecasts depend on the backtest adjustment; raw forecasts and recipe differences are in the details.

[![Paloma scaling comparison with measured finals and d1536 forecasts](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/h100-mix25-paloma/2026.09.14.2/paloma-scaling-bpb.png)](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/h100-mix25-paloma/2026.09.14.2/index.html)

[Interactive plot](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/h100-mix25-paloma/2026.09.14.2/index.html). Filled gold: measured final new-mixture d768/d1024; hollow gold: forecast d1536 at 100% of training, adjusted using smaller-run backtests. Blue: measured final original-mixture d768/d1024/d1536. Labels show compute-equivalent speedup: **1.20×** means the original-mixture baseline needs 20% more compute to match that point’s quality. d512 is omitted to keep the y-axis range focused on the larger models.

## Mixture phases

- **0–25%:** Harrier, emphasizing software, science, history, and math.
- **25–80%:** More command-line agent transcripts, law, and news; less general web code, finance, history, and math.
- **80–100%:** More natural-science research and data in the highest classifier-rated quality bucket, while retaining the emphasis on low-level code and agent transcripts.

Percentages refer to training steps; transitions round to mixture-block boundaries.

<details>
<summary>Phase weights, topic labels, and quality shares</summary>

Each phase weights 200 topic × quality groups. Topic shares below sum over quality buckets; quality shares sum over topics. Topic names describe the dominant content in each cluster, using the [store’s labels and examples](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling).

- **Start to 25% — Harrier:** Software-heavy, led by infrastructure/security (9.3%), performance logs and low-level code (9.0%), and natural-science research (8.8%). General software development/web code contributes 7.9%; history/literature 6.9%; math problems/proofs 4.3%.
- **25% to roughly 80% — new phase 0:** More command-line agent transcripts (1.3% → 6.0%), law/courts (1.1% → 3.6%), and world news (0.8% → 2.7%). Less general software development/web code (7.9% → 4.5%), finance (5.6% → 2.4%), history/literature (6.9% → 3.7%), and math (4.3% → 1.8%). Performance logs and low-level code become the largest cluster at 10.6%.
- **Roughly 80% to finish — new phase 1:** More natural-science research (6.9% → 11.3%), alongside performance logs/low-level code (11.4%) and agent transcripts (6.6%). General software development/web code falls again, to 3.1%, and math to 1.4%. The highest classifier-rated quality bucket, Q4, rises from 22.9% to 28.0% of the mixture; it was 22.6% in the initial phase.

Arrows compare each phase with the preceding phase. These are configured weights, not measured token counts or claims that every document matches its cluster’s label. [All 40 topic shares and five quality shares](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/h100-mix25-paloma/mixture-phases-2026.09.13.1/index.html).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Forecast method, backtest errors, and projected speedups</summary>

Updated September 14 using the 60–80% evaluations, through step 72,607: **2.55421 final loss / 0.92256 BPB** after the backtest adjustment, versus **2.56377 / 0.92507** for the baseline. That projects **0.27% lower BPB**, or **1.07× compute-equivalent speedup** at equal throughput. The prior adjusted forecast was 2.55604 / 0.92292. [Forecast and backtests](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/h100-mix25-paloma/forecast-2026.09.14.2/index.html).

Fit a line to d1536’s 60%, 65%, 70%, 75%, and 80% evaluations and extrapolate to 100%, following Larry’s linear procedure. Backtest the same window on each completed smaller run. The 80% evaluation is just after the cooldown mixture switch at step 72,576; almost all cooldown training remains unobserved.

| Estimate | Final macro loss | Final macro BPB |
|---|---:|---:|
| Raw linear projection | 2.54480 | 0.91882 |
| Plus mean d768/d1024 backtest error | 2.55421 | 0.92256 |
| Completed original-mixture d1536 baseline | 2.56377 | 0.92507 |

The adjustment uses d768 and d1024, the two nearest completed widths. The fit underpredicts their final losses by 0.01179 and 0.00702. The adjusted forecast adds their mean, 0.00941; the BPB adjustment is +0.00375. These backtests include the same mixture transitions, but transferring their residuals to d1536 is an assumption. d512’s loss error is 0.00702 and is reported separately.

The raw macro-BPB forecast implies 1.18× compute-equivalent speedup; the adjusted forecast implies 1.07×. These are point estimates, not confidence bounds. The report includes all 16 subset forecasts, speedups, frozen evaluations, and checks using 50–80% and 70–80% windows. [Previous 70%-based forecast](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/h100-mix25-paloma/forecast-2026.09.14.1/index.html).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Swarm comparison: measured endpoints, speedup assumptions, and Uncheatable</summary>

The [pinned swarm snapshot](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/grug-moe-mix-swarm/tree/75c25718e2a7cf7a3b1b498b00479351f80345e0/registry/v1/swarms/h100-d512-from10pct-store-4d2e363d) contains three seeds of the selected `996f489106c7b922` mixture and three seeds of the old Harrier mixture. The selected weights match the ladder’s `best_mixture_996f489106c7b922.json` exactly; old weights match `harrier_mix_2026_08_18.json` within 1.1e-8 per cell. All six runs restore the same step-393 checkpoint after 10% baseline training, then train at the same d512 budget. Metrics below are means of final dropless BPB, not surrogate predictions.

| Evaluation | Old mix BPB | Selected mix BPB | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Macro Paloma | 1.193383 | 1.186012 | −0.62% |
| Code: 100 programming languages | 0.704489 | 0.678921 | −3.63% |
| Academic documents: M2D2 S2ORC | 0.953385 | 0.947892 | −0.58% |
| Falcon RefinedWeb | 1.110216 | 1.105921 | −0.39% |
| Dolma v1.5 | 1.002632 | 0.995775 | −0.68% |
| Macro Uncheatable | 0.877434 | 0.864898 | −1.43% |
| Uncheatable C++ | 0.603348 | 0.572521 | −5.11% |
| Uncheatable Python | 0.548619 | 0.537162 | −2.09% |
| Uncheatable arXiv computer science | 0.877615 | 0.861141 | −1.88% |
| Uncheatable arXiv physics | 0.950631 | 0.922505 | −2.96% |

Paloma compute-equivalent speedup is `(old mean BPB / selected mean BPB)^(1/α)` at equal compute and throughput. It uses the original d768/d1024/d1536 ladder’s per-subset slopes, with zero loss floor; macro α is 0.040007. Applying those slopes at d512 is an assumption, and this swarm helped select the mixture, so it is not independent validation. No Uncheatable multiplier is inferred from Paloma slopes.

[All measured comparisons and calculation inputs](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/h100-mix25-paloma/swarm-2026.09.14.1/comparison.csv) · [Six source observations](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/h100-mix25-paloma/swarm-2026.09.14.1/selected_runs.json) · [Reproduction script](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/h100-mix25-paloma/swarm-2026.09.14.1/analyze.py) · [Input files](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/h100-mix25-paloma/swarm-2026.09.14.1/index.html).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Measured results, pre-swap comparison, and speedup calculation</summary>

Snapshot: September 13, 1:10 p.m. Pacific. d512, d768, and d1024 have finished.

| Final macro BPB | Baseline | New mixture | Change | Subsets improved |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| d768 | 1.083720 | 1.079330 | −0.41% | 11/16 |
| d1024 | 1.002217 | 0.995244 | −0.70% | 12/16 |

Macro BPB is the mean across all 16 subsets. At d768, the largest improvements are Twitter AAE (−1.47%), 4chan (−1.22%), and Gab (−0.92%). RedPajama (+1.28%), Penn Treebank (+0.77%), Wikipedia (+0.46%), WikiText (+0.29%), and programming languages (+0.28%) regress. Lower BPB is better.

At d1024, the largest improvements are Twitter AAE (−2.04%), Gab (−1.54%), and 4chan (−1.18%). RedPajama (+0.82%), Wikipedia (+0.37%), WikiText (+0.30%), and programming languages (+0.06%) regress.

The d768 treatment was already 0.61% lower in macro BPB at 20% training, before the switch. Both d768 runs use the same batch and total token budget, so this compares matched token counts. Validation data match across all 16 subsets. Hardware, expert-parallel size, evaluation batch, and some optimizer settings differ; the frozen configurations record the details.

The d512 coordinator repeated its final evaluation after a retry. The comparison uses one final point per run; see the [incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/416).

The speedup calculation recenters and inverts each subset’s plotted baseline fit, following the [MoE guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/experiments/grug/moe/agent.md#effective-speedup-calculation). It uses the subset fit’s exponent and zero loss floor, replacing the guide’s macro-loss constants. [Calculation inputs and results](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/h100-mix25-paloma/2026.09.14.2/point_speedups.csv).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Run configurations, source metadata, and earlier analyses</summary>

The initial mixture is Harrier 2026.08.18. The data store and simulated epoching stay the same.

All treatment runs use sequence length 4,096, global batch 1,024, and 791 training tokens per active parameter. The d-number is model hidden width. Phase 0 and phase 1 below are the new mixture's two weight sets.

| Rung / W&B run | H100 GPUs | Total steps | New phase 0 starts | New phase 1 starts |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [d512](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/h100-mix25-20260912-d512) | 8 | 3,930 | 1,008 | 3,120 |
| [d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/h100-mix25-20260912-d768) | 16 | 11,420 | 2,880 | 9,120 |
| [d1024](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/h100-mix25-20260912-d1024) | 32 | 30,552 | 7,680 | 24,432 |
| [d1536](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/h100-mix25-20260912-d1536) | 64 | 90,767 | 22,704 | 72,576 |

The launcher is `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_h100_scaling_ladder.py`; weights are in `best_mixture_996f489106c7b922.json` beside it, extracted from `best-mixture-996f489106c7b922.parquet`. The exact launch source and weights have not yet been published. Mixture metadata: swarm `h100-d512-from10pct-store-4d2e363d`, HF revision `75c25718e2a7cf7a3b1b498b00479351f80345e0`.

- [Original hero scaling report](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng), tracked in #8435.
- [Frozen run configurations and evaluation history](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/issue-9126-paloma-20260912-1220).
- [Earlier 50%-progress analysis](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/Paloma-scaling-comparison:-mixture-switch-after-25%-of-training--VmlldzoxNzkyMTA0MQ==), retained for the pre-swap comparisons.

</details>

## Next steps

- [ ] Refresh the d1536 forecast, then compare with its measured final endpoint.
- [ ] Publish the exact launch source and mixture weights.
- [ ] Record Monday’s target run/checkpoint, acceptable subset regressions, and proceed/defer decision.

spillover_issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment tested whether packed vLLM rollout inference could improve Iris RL throughput on `v5p` by running `2 x TP=2` inference inside one rollout worker. `PKR-001` validated the packed path end-to-end, but it did not beat the direct `e4ms2` topology: trainer cadence was about `171s/step` versus about `101s/step` for `e4ms2`, largely because evaluation still monopolized the rollout job. Follow-up runs showed the packed sampler itself is viable, especially when eval is sparse, but normal `eval_frequency=1` reintroduced enough contention that packed rollout was not promoted as the default RL topology. The current recommendation is to keep packed vLLM as validated follow-up work, not a replacement, until train/eval routing or scheduling removes that contention.

### Helpful links
- https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/3960
- https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_iris_rl_debug/runs/e4ms2-20260326-121919-train
- https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_iris_rl_debug/runs/pkr001-20260327-012712-train
- https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_iris_rl_debug/runs/pkr003-20260327-072722-train
- https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_iris_rl_debug/runs/pkr004-20260327-094215-train
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Direct packed RL on Iris is now real, but it is not yet a promoted replacement for direct `e4ms2`. `PKR-001` proved one `v5p-8` rollout worker can host packed `2 x TP=2` inference end-to-end, but trainer cadence landed near `e4par` because eval still monopolized the single rollout job. Later eval-isolated follow-ups (`PKR-003`, `PKR-004`) showed the packed sampler path itself is healthy, but normal `eval_frequency=1` still reintroduces enough contention to block promotion.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Packed vLLM should become the higher-leverage RL inference path on `v5p` if train/eval routing and scheduling preserve enough trainer-facing cadence to beat single-rollout parity and get close enough to direct `e4ms2` to justify promotion.

### Links

* #3959
* PR: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/3960
* Baseline `e4ms2`: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_iris_rl_debug/runs/e4ms2-20260326-121919-train
* `PKR-001` trainer: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_iris_rl_debug/runs/pkr001-20260327-012712-train
* `PKR-001` rollout: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_iris_rl_debug/runs/pkr001-20260327-012712-rollout-0
* `PKR-003` trainer: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_iris_rl_debug/runs/pkr003-20260327-072722-train
* `PKR-003` rollout: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_iris_rl_debug/runs/pkr003-20260327-072722-rollout-0
* `PKR-004` trainer: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_iris_rl_debug/runs/pkr004-20260327-094215-train
* `PKR-004` rollout: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_iris_rl_debug/runs/pkr004-20260327-094215-rollout-0

## Results

`PKR-001` was a correctness success and a throughput miss: steady cadence was about `171s/step` vs direct `e4ms2` at about `101s/step`. `PKR-003` succeeded with sparse eval and looked materially healthier. `PKR-004` also succeeded under normal eval cadence, but the same eval-heavy contention pattern returned. Current status: packed rollout is validated, but not yet promoted as the default RL topology.
